Or is it just a word we use, or just an idea in our heads? Philosophers have three standard answers, and chapter 3 needs you to know them, because its whole argument is that two of the three fail.
summary.body:
Look around a pool hall. There are many individual cues, many individual balls, one rack. Yet each cue is an instance of the same pattern, *being a pool cue*. Several balls share the pattern *redness* with stop signs and strawberries; all of them share *roundness* with basketballs and the moon; the rack shares *triangularity* with pyramids and dunce caps. Philosophers call such shared patterns **universals** — one pattern that many particular things can exhibit.

They are called **abstract** because in considering them we abstract from — leave out — the individualizing features of concrete things: that this triangle is wooden and green, that one metal and orange. An **abstract object**, in the philosopher’s sense, is not vague or hazy; it is something real that is not located in space, cannot be seen or touched, and does not enter into causal transactions. Chapter 3 identifies four families: **universals** (redness, triangularity, humanness); **propositions** (what a statement says, as opposed to the sentence used to say it — “Snow is white” and “Schnee ist weiss” are two sentences expressing one proposition); **numbers** and other mathematical objects (the numeral “2” is a label, not the number); and **possible worlds** (complete ways things could have been).

Now the three positions.

**Realism** says universals are real and exist independently of the human mind. Triangles would still all be three-sided if no one were around to notice.

**Nominalism** (from Latin *nomen*, name) says only particular things exist; “redness” is just a name, a convenient label we apply to a bunch of individuals. There is no such thing as redness itself.

**Conceptualism** says universals exist, but only as concepts in human minds. Triangularity is something we make when we form a general idea.

Chapter 3 argues that nominalism and conceptualism both fail, for reasons a beginner can appreciate. Mathematical and logical truths hold whether or not any human being thinks them; they held before there were humans and would hold if humanity vanished. Erase every instance of the sentence “Snow is white” in every language and the proposition it expressed is still true. So these things cannot be human concepts, and they cannot be mere names, because names are things we make.

But Feser also rejects the most famous version of realism. **Plato** placed the universals in a realm of their own — a “third realm” beside minds and physical things. Chapter 3 argues that this is unsatisfactory: such objects would be causally inert and disconnected from everything, and it becomes mysterious how we could ever come to know them. The alternative, developed from Augustine, is called **Scholastic realism**: universals and other abstract objects are real and mind-independent with respect to *our* minds, but they exist as ideas in an intellect — a divine intellect. That is the conclusion of the Augustinian proof.
summary.takeaway: Universals are the patterns many things share; realism says they are real independently of us, nominalism says they are only names, conceptualism says they are only human concepts — and chapter 3 argues that only a realism grounding them in a divine intellect survives.
summary.deepDive:
**Why this feels strange at first, and why it shouldn’t.** Beginners often think the question is verbal fussing. Try this test instead. Before any human being existed, was it true that seven is prime, and that nothing can be both round and square? Almost everyone says yes. But if a truth requires a proposition, and a proposition is neither a physical object nor a human thought, then something real existed before us that was neither physical nor human-mental. That is not a trick; it is a genuine tension in the ordinary view of the world, and chapter 3 is the attempt to relieve it.

**A worked example: the proposition versus the sentence.** Write “Snow is white” on a whiteboard. You can see the sentence — the ink. Now write “Schnee ist weiss.” Different ink, different shapes, same thing said. What you can see is the sentence; what the two share is the proposition. Erase both. Has the proposition stopped being true? Clearly not. So the proposition is not the ink. Nor is it your thought about snow, since your thought and mine are numerically different acts while what we think is the same. This is what motivates treating propositions as abstract objects.

**The three positions as answers to one question.** Ask: when Socrates and Fido are both animals, what makes that true? The nominalist says: nothing beyond Socrates and Fido plus our habit of applying one word. The conceptualist says: our concept *animal*, which we formed. The realist says: a genuine pattern that both instantiate. Feser’s worry about the first two is the same in both cases — they make the truths of logic, mathematics, and science depend on us, when those truths are precisely the ones that seem most independent of us.

**A nuance that trips people up.** “Mind-independent” in this debate means independent of *human* minds. Scholastic realism says universals are mind-independent in that sense while still existing in a mind — God’s. That is not a contradiction, though it sounds like one until you notice the qualification.

**How it feeds the arguments.** Chapter 3 is the only one of the five that is not a causal argument at all, which is why Feser notes in chapter 7 that “what caused God?” is not even prima facie relevant to it. Its conclusion — a necessarily existing intellect — is then shown in chapter 6 to be the same God the other four proofs reach.

**The usual confusion.** People assume “abstract object” means “imaginary” or “made up.” In philosophy it means the opposite of concrete: real, but not in space and time, and not causally interacting.

checks.q: Nominalism is the view that…
options: universals exist only as concepts in human minds
universals exist in a realm of their own, apart from all minds
only particular things exist; universals are merely names we apply
universals exist as ideas in a divine intellect
checks.explanation: Nominalism (from Latin nomen, name) denies that there is anything real corresponding to general terms. The other options describe conceptualism, Platonic realism, and Scholastic realism respectively.

checks.q: Why does Feser think propositions cannot be merely human thoughts?
options: because human thoughts are private
because propositions can be written in many languages
because thoughts can be false and propositions cannot
because truths such as mathematical ones held before humans existed and would hold if humanity vanished
checks.explanation: Conceptualism makes abstract truths depend on us, but such truths seem to hold independently of whether anyone ever thinks them. That is the key objection developed in chapter 3.

checks.q: Feser’s Augustinian proof rejects Plato’s version of realism mainly because…
options: a realm of causally inert objects standing apart from everything leaves it mysterious how they relate to the world and how we know them
Plato’s Forms are too few in number
universals turn out not to exist after all
Plato was not a Christian
checks.explanation: The objection is philosophical, not biographical: a free-floating third realm is disconnected and epistemically inaccessible. Grounding the objects in an intellect solves both problems.

summary.heading: 12. Parts and composition: what “simple” means in philosophy
summary.plain: In ordinary speech “simple” means easy. In philosophy it means something completely different: having no parts at all. A thing with parts depends on those parts and on whatever holds them together — so if something is going to be the ultimate explanation of everything else, it had better not be made of anything.
summary.takeaway: A composite thing depends at every moment on its parts and on whatever unites them, so the ultimate cause must be simple — having no parts at all, physical or metaphysical — which is why the five proofs converge on one and the same conclusion.
summary.deepDive:
**The explanatory-circle argument, slowly.** The chair exists only because its parts exist and are arranged chairwise at this moment. Could the chair itself be what arranges them? No: to do any arranging it would have to exist already, and its existing already presupposes the arrangement. So we would be explaining the arrangement by something whose existence the arrangement explains — a vicious circle. Hence something *outside* the composite must account for the union of its parts. Chapter 2 then asks what accounts for *that* thing, generating a hierarchical series that can only terminate in something with no parts to be united in the first place.

**Why “metaphysical parts” is not cheating.** A newcomer may protest: form and matter are not parts the way legs are; you cannot put them in separate boxes. Correct — and the tradition agrees. They are called **principles**: really distinct aspects within one thing, neither of which exists on its own. The argument does not need them to be separable. It needs only that they are really distinct, so that their being together in one thing is a fact requiring explanation. That is exactly the point chapter 4 establishes for essence and existence.

**A worked example.** Consider yourself. You have physical parts (organs). You have matter and a form organizing it. You have accidents (your current mood) distinct from you. You have potentials (to learn Greek) unrealized. You have an essence, and the separate fact that you exist. Six kinds of composition, each of which is a dependency. Remove them all and what is left is not a very impressive being — it is not a being of that sort at all. That is the point of insisting that God is not an item on the list of things, but sheer actuality.

**The qualification Feser adds.** Simplicity does not mean God lacks the perfections we attribute to him, or that our different words for God are all synonyms. It means those perfections are not distinct constituents. The hardest form of this objection comes from Alvin Plantinga, who argues that if God is identical with each of his properties then God has only one property and is himself a property — an abstract object. Chapter 6 answers that this misreads the doctrine by importing a Platonic account of properties and a univocal account of religious language, neither of which classical theists accept.

**How it feeds the argument.** This is what secures the simplicity conclusion of chapter 2 and, by way of it, the immutability, immateriality, eternity and unity of God that the later stages derive.

**The usual confusion.** People read “God is simple” as “God is easy to understand,” which is nearly the reverse of the truth. Feser holds that God is **incomprehensible** — not fully graspable by a finite intellect — precisely because of what simplicity involves.

checks.q: In philosophy, to say something is “simple” means that it…
options: has no parts of any kind
is easy to understand
has only one physical part
is uncomplicated in behaviour
checks.explanation: Philosophical simplicity is non-compositeness — no physical or metaphysical parts. It has nothing to do with ease of understanding; Feser in fact holds God to be incomprehensible.

checks.q: Which of the following counts as a metaphysical part?
options: a chair’s legs
an animal’s heart
the distinction between a thing’s essence and its existence
a book’s pages
checks.explanation: Metaphysical parts are really distinct principles within one thing — form and matter, essence and existence, act and potency — not separable physical components.

checks.q: Why can’t a composite thing be the cause of its own parts being united?
options: because parts are always older than wholes
because that would be circular: the whole exists only given the union it is supposed to explain
because composites have no causal powers at all
because the parts might be infinite in number
checks.explanation: The whole’s existence presupposes that the parts are already combined, so it cannot be what combines them. Something distinct from the composite must account for the union.

summary.heading: 13. Classical theism versus “a very powerful being”: the single biggest source of confusion
summary.plain: Most arguments about God go nowhere because the two sides mean different things by the word. Many people — believers and atheists alike — picture God as an extremely impressive being: very powerful, very knowing, very good, but still a being, one item among the things that exist. That is not what this book is defending. Classical theism says God is not an item in the universe’s inventory at all, but pure actuality, the source of the existence of everything else.
summary.body:
Here is the view Feser defends, attribute by attribute, in the plainest terms available.

- **Pure actuality**: God has no unrealized potentials. He is not a thing that *could* become something else. All the other attributes fall out of this one.
- **Simplicity**: no parts, physical or metaphysical. God’s essence just *is* his existence; his power and knowledge are not distinct components.
- **Immutability**: unchanging — because to change is to have a potential actualized, and there are none.
- **Eternity**: not merely everlasting in time, but outside time altogether. Something in time undergoes change, and God does not.
- **Necessity**: could not possibly have failed to exist, because there is nothing in him that could have been otherwise.
- **Omnipotence**: being that from which all causal power derives — not “can do absolutely anything, including contradictions.”
- **Omniscience**: knowing all things, because the forms or patterns of everything caused must in some way be in the cause.
- **Perfect goodness**: to fall short of goodness is to fail to actualize something one could have; pure actuality has no such shortfall.
- **Immateriality and incorporeality**: matter involves potentiality, so what is purely actual cannot be material.
- **Unity**: there cannot even in principle be two such beings, since differentiating them would require a feature one has and the other lacks — and each would then be “pure actuality PLUS something,” hence not pure actuality.

Now the contrast. Philosophers have coined the labels **theistic personalism** and **neo-theism** for a family of contemporary views that treat God as, in effect, the unique member of a species falling under the genus *person*, alongside human beings and angels, differing from them by lacking their limitations in power, knowledge, and goodness. Feser is careful about what the disagreement is and is not. It is **not** that classical theists deny God is personal — most attribute intellect and will to God and regard him as personal. The disagreement is that theistic personalists take God’s being personal to entail that he falls under a genus, and so is not simple. Some go further: process theologians such as Charles Hartshorne deny God is immutable, holding that God changes as persons do. But to be changeable is to have potentials as well as actualities, and so to be composite rather than simple.

Why does this matter so much for a beginner? Because almost every popular objection to theism is aimed at the personalist picture. “God is just a bigger version of us.” “Who designed the designer?” “God is an unnecessary extra entity — Ockham’s razor shaves him off.” Each of these presupposes that God is one being among others, subject to the same questions. Against classical theism they do not land, because the arguments conclude to something that could not in principle be another item in the inventory.

Feser makes the point with real force: on classical theist premises, to deny that anything is simple or non-composite would effectively be to deny that there is anything with the ultimacy that makes something God at all.
summary.takeaway: Classical theism holds that God is pure actuality — simple, immutable, eternal, necessary, omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good, and the unique source of all power and existence — not an extremely impressive being alongside others, which is what theistic personalism makes him.
summary.deepDive:
**Getting the disagreement exactly right.** It is tempting, and wrong, to summarize the difference as “classical theists think God is impersonal.” Feser explicitly denies this. Classical theists attribute intellect and will to God; the Augustinian proof concludes to a divine *intellect*. The real difference is structural: does God fall under a genus, as one kind of person among possible kinds? If yes, he has an essence distinct from what differentiates him within the genus, hence composition, hence dependence — and hence, on the arguments of this book, he is not the ultimate explanation at all but one more thing needing one.

**Why omnipotence is not “can do anything.”** A beginner asked whether God can make a square circle usually expects a squirm. The classical answer is that a square circle is not a thing God cannot do; it is not a thing at all — the words describe nothing. Feser’s derivation is more interesting than the usual formula: to have power is to be able to actualize potentials; every actualized potential traces to the purely actual actualizer; therefore all power derives from it; and to be that from which all power derives is what omnipotence means. Omnipotence is thus a *conclusion*, not a definition chosen in advance.

**A worked example of the confusion in action.** Someone says: “Adding God to your explanation of the universe violates Ockham’s razor — you have posited an extra entity.” Notice the assumption: God is an entity, of the same general sort as electrons and galaxies, and we are counting. On classical theism, what the arguments conclude to is not a further item on the list but that in virtue of which anything is on the list at all. Whether the arguments succeed is a fair question; whether they posit an ordinary extra entity is not.

**Why the derivations matter more than the list.** You could memorize the ten attributes and still miss the point. Almost all of them are derived from pure actuality by the same move: attribute X would require an unactualized potential; there are none; therefore X’s opposite. That is the pattern of steps 19–32 in chapter 1’s formal argument. If you learn the pattern you can reconstruct the list.

**The usual confusion.** People assume classical theism is a later, colder, more abstract development, and personalism the original, warm, biblical view. Feser argues the reverse: divine simplicity is the mainstream of the Western tradition across pagan, Jewish, Muslim, and Christian thinkers and was taught as binding doctrine by two Catholic councils; theistic personalism is the recent departure.

checks.q: What distinguishes theistic personalism from classical theism?
options: theistic personalism denies God exists
classical theism denies God is personal, while theistic personalism affirms it
theistic personalism takes God to fall under a genus and so to be composite rather than simple
classical theism denies God is good
checks.explanation: Feser is explicit that the difference is not over whether God is personal — most classical theists attribute intellect and will to God. It is over whether God falls under a genus and is composite.

checks.q: In classical theism, God’s eternity means that God…
options: will exist for an infinitely long time
exists outside of time altogether, since existing in time would involve change
began at the Big Bang and continues forever
experiences time faster than we do
checks.explanation: Eternity here is timelessness, not endless duration. Step 22 of chapter 1’s argument reasons that existing in time would involve change, which pure actuality excludes.

checks.q: An atheist argues: “Positing God adds an extra entity, so Ockham’s razor tells against it.” The classical theist’s most accurate reply is:
options: Ockham’s razor is a discredited principle
God is a simpler entity than the universe, so the razor favours theism
the argument concludes not to a further item in the inventory of things but to that in virtue of which anything exists at all
we should multiply entities whenever it is convenient
checks.explanation: The objection presupposes the theistic-personalist picture of God as one being among others. Classical theism denies that framing; the conclusion is the source of existence, not another instance of it.

summary.heading: 14. Analogy: univocal, equivocal, and analogical talk about God
summary.plain: If God is nothing like anything else, how can our words apply to him at all? The classical answer is that words like “good” and “wise” are used of God neither in exactly the sense they have for us, nor in a totally unrelated sense, but in a related, stretched sense — the way “good” means something different yet related in “good wine” and “good man.” That middle option is called analogy, and getting it straight defuses a surprising number of objections.
summary.body:
There are three ways a word can be used across two cases.

**Univocal** — exactly the same sense. “Fido is a dog” and “Rover is a dog.” The word means one thing in both.

**Equivocal** — completely different and unrelated senses that happen to share a spelling. “A bat flew around the attic” and “I swung the bat at it.” Nothing but the noise is shared.

**Analogical** — an in-between usage: related but not identical senses. “This wine is still good” and “George is a good man.” The goodness of wine is not the goodness of a man; a good man is not merely un-spoiled. Yet the two are not unrelated either: in each case something is functioning well and completely as the kind of thing it is.

Classical theists say our talk of God is **analogical**. When we call God good, wise, or powerful, we are not saying he has exactly what we call goodness, wisdom and power in us — that would be univocal talk, and would make God a being of our kind with the limits removed. Nor are we speaking pure nonsense or metaphor — that would be equivocal, and would make theology empty noise. We are saying that there is in God something genuinely analogous to what goodness and knowledge are in us.

Two points that Feser is careful about and that beginners usually get wrong.

First: **analogical is not the same as metaphorical.** When we say “God is a rock,” that is metaphor. When we say “God is good,” that is a *literal* claim used analogically. Feser objects to Plantinga's rendering of Aquinas’ view as the thesis that our language about God is “analogical rather than literal.” Non-univocal does not entail non-literal.

Second: **analogy is also at work far below theology.** Feser introduces it in chapter 2 and develops it in chapter 6 under the heading “the analogy of being.” Consider a stone and the stone's colour and shape. Both the stone and its colour are real — but the reality of a colour is not the same kind of reality as the reality of a stone, since a colour exists only *in* something else. We use “real” and “exists” analogically all the time without noticing.

Why does this matter so much? Because a great many objections to classical theism are powered by an unnoticed assumption of univocity. If “knowledge” and “power” mean in God precisely what they mean in us, then since our knowledge and our power are distinct things, God's must be too — and divine simplicity collapses. That is exactly the shape of Plantinga’s objection in chapter 6, and Feser's reply is that the assumption of univocity is not one classical theists ever granted. Similarly, if “person” means the same for God and for us, then God is one more person among persons, and the atheist’s “one god further” jibe gets traction. Analogy blocks these moves not by evasion but by insisting on a distinction the tradition drew long before the objections were framed.
summary.takeaway: Words applied to God are used neither univocally (the same sense as in us) nor equivocally (an unrelated sense) but analogically — a related, literal, stretched sense — and many standard objections to classical theism quietly assume univocity.
summary.deepDive:
**The pressure that makes analogy necessary.** Run the alternatives and watch both fail. Suppose our words apply to God univocally. Then God's goodness is the same kind of thing as human goodness, differing only in degree. But human goodness is an accident of a composite being, limited and capable of increase. A God of whom that is literally true is composite, and the arguments of chapters 1–5 show that such a thing needs a cause. Now suppose our words apply equivocally. Then calling God good conveys no more than calling him *blorp*; every theological sentence becomes noise, and the conclusions of the proofs would be unstatable. Analogy is what is left when both extremes are excluded — not a convenient fudge, but the only remaining option.

**A worked example to run on yourself.** Take “healthy.” A person is healthy. A diet is healthy. A complexion is healthy. These are not the same sense: a diet does not have a pulse. But they are not unrelated either — the diet causes health, the complexion signifies it, the person possesses it. The tradition calls this the **analogy of attribution**. Something similar happens with “good,” where the relation is one of proportion rather than causation: as a knife’s sharpness is to a knife, so a person’s justice is to a person. That is the **analogy of proper proportionality**. You do not need to memorize the labels, but you should notice that ordinary language already does this constantly and nobody finds it mysterious.

**The nuance Feser insists on.** Analogical predication is literal. To say “God is wise” is to make a true, literal claim about God. What is denied is only that “wise” carries precisely the content it carries when said of Socrates. Keep those apart and you will avoid the common misreading that classical theism is a genteel form of agnosticism.

**How it feeds the arguments.** Analogy is one of three background principles Feser sets out at the start of chapter 6, alongside the principle of proportionate causality and *agere sequitur esse*. All three are then used to derive the divine attributes from the nature of the world considered as an effect. Without analogy, the derivations in chapter 1’s steps 28–47 would generate contradictions rather than conclusions.

**The usual confusion.** People take “we speak of God analogically” to mean “we don’t really know what we are saying.” It means almost the opposite: we know what we are saying, and we also know that the reality exceeds the way our concepts carve it up.

checks.q: “There was a bat in the attic” and “I swung the bat.” This is an example of…
options: equivocal use
univocal use
analogical use
metaphorical use
checks.explanation: Equivocal terms share only a spelling or sound; the senses are wholly unrelated. Univocal use would be identical sense, analogical a related but not identical sense.

checks.q: Feser insists that analogical language about God is…
options: purely metaphorical
literal, though not univocal
univocal but imprecise
meaningless but psychologically useful
checks.explanation: Non-univocal does not entail non-literal. Feser criticises the characterization of Aquinas’ view as the thesis that God-talk is analogical rather than literal; the analogy of attribution and of proper proportionality are literal uses.

checks.q: An objector argues: “Power and knowledge are distinct in us, so they must be distinct in God; divine simplicity is therefore incoherent.” Which assumption is doing the work?
options: that God exists
that knowledge is a kind of power
that God has parts
that ‘power’ and ‘knowledge’ apply univocally to God and to us
checks.explanation: The inference only goes through if the terms mean exactly the same thing in both cases. Classical theists apply them analogically, so what is distinct in us need not be distinct in God.

summary.heading: 15. How to read Feser’s book: the two-stage pattern, the fifty-step wall, and a routine that works
summary.plain: The book has a repeating shape, and once you see it you will always know where you are. Each of the first five chapters tells the argument twice — first in a relaxed, chatty way, then as a numbered list — and then answers objections. The numbered lists can look terrifying. They are not; they are just a summary of what you already read, in bullet form. Here is a routine for getting through it without panic.
summary.body:
**The architecture.** Feser explains it himself in the Introduction, and it holds for chapters 1 through 5.

1. **Informal statement, Stage 1** — a discursive, leisurely argument that something exists fitting a key description: a purely actual actualizer, an absolutely simple cause, a divine intellect, a cause whose essence is existence, a necessary being.
2. **Informal statement, Stage 2** — an argument that anything fitting that description must have the divine attributes: unity, immateriality, eternity, omnipotence, omniscience, perfect goodness. This is the stage that answers “sure, but why call *that* God?”
3. **Formal statement** — the same reasoning as an explicit numbered list, so the logical structure is visible. Chapter 1’s runs to fifty steps.
4. **Objections** — often the most technical material in the chapter.

Feser describes the method as starting at the shallowest part of the shallow end and ending in the deepest part of the deep end. Expect that. If a chapter gets hard near the end, that is the design working, not you failing.

**How to face a fifty-step argument calmly.** Four habits help enormously.

- **Remember it is a recap.** The formal statement introduces no new material. If a step baffles you, the explanation is in the informal pages you already read.
- **Find the joints.** Long arguments come in blocks. In chapter 1: steps 1–5 set up change and the principle of causality; 6–14 run the hierarchical-series argument to a purely actual actualizer; 15–18 establish uniqueness; and 19–47 derive the attributes one at a time. Nobody reads fifty steps as fifty; read four blocks.
- **Label every step.** Each is a premise, an inference, or the conclusion. For inferences, write in the margin which earlier steps it comes from. Steps beginning “So,” are inferences; they need no independent defence, only a valid link.
- **Attack, don’t absorb.** After each block ask: which single step here would I challenge first? Even if you end up agreeing, you will understand far more.

**A reading routine for each module of this course.**

1. **Prepare here.** Read the module’s plain-English summaries, then the full bodies, then the deep dives. Do the section checks.
2. **Watch the video.** Each module has a study document for NotebookLM, which will generate a video overview. Watch it before reading the chapter, as an orientation.
3. **Read the chapter**, using the module’s reading map to know which pages deserve slow attention and which can be skimmed first time.
4. **Come back and practise.** Work the argument walkthrough, the objections, the quiz, the flashcards, and the teach-back challenge.

**Taking notes that are worth having.** Skip highlighting; it feels productive and teaches little. Instead keep a running page with four columns for each chapter: *terms* (word, one-line definition, the page where it was introduced); *steps* (the numbered argument in your own compressed words); *objections* (objection, reply, how convinced you are, 1–5); and *questions* (things you did not follow, with page numbers, to revisit after the chapter). If you can produce those four columns for a chapter, you have understood it.
summary.takeaway: Every proof chapter runs informal Stage 1, informal Stage 2, formal numbered statement, then objections — so the numbered argument is always a recap, best read in blocks with each step labelled as premise, inference, or conclusion.
summary.deepDive:
**Why the two stages exist, and why Stage 2 is the one people skip.** Beginners often stop at Stage 1, satisfied or unsatisfied, and never engage Stage 2. That is a mistake, because the standard complaint — “even if you got to some first cause, why think it’s *God*, rather than a brute force or an undetected particle?” — is exactly what Stage 2 answers. Feser's strategy is to show that anything fitting the Stage 1 description must, by the same metaphysics, be one, immaterial, eternal, omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good. If you do not follow Stage 2 you will not be able to answer the most common objection you will meet in conversation.

**Working a formal step properly — a demonstration.** Take step 11 of chapter 1: a regress of concurrent actualizers would constitute a hierarchical causal series, and such a series cannot regress infinitely. Ask four questions of it. *What kind of step is it?* A premise, resting on the earlier informal argument. *What does it claim, in my own words?* That a stack of borrowers cannot go on forever, because borrowing never creates what is borrowed. *What is the natural objection?* That an infinite series needs no first member — every member has a predecessor, so every member is accounted for. *What is the reply?* That this works for linear series but not hierarchical ones: an infinitely long paintbrush handle still does not paint, and an infinite stack of desks holds up nothing. Four questions, three minutes, and the step is yours. Do that for the steps that carry weight — usually the premises, rarely the inferences.

**What to skim on a first pass.** Feser says the objection sections are in some cases where the most technical material appears. On a first read of chapter 1 you can skim the discussions of Newton, Einstein and quantum mechanics (roughly pages 43–63) and return later; the same goes for Kenny’s objection in chapter 4 and the Leftow and Grim material in chapter 3. Skimming with intent to return is a reading strategy, not a retreat.

**A pacing suggestion.** At perhaps twelve to fifteen pages an hour with notes, chapter 1 is four or five sittings, not one. Chapter 6 is eighty pages and should be split; this course splits it into two modules for exactly that reason.

**The usual confusion.** People treat the numbered argument as the real argument and the informal pages as throat-clearing. It is closer to the reverse: the informal statement carries the justification, the numbered statement carries the structure. You need both, and you should read them in that order.

checks.q: In each of the first five chapters, what does Stage 2 of the informal statement do?
options: argues that whatever fits the Stage 1 description must have the divine attributes
answers objections from critics
restates the argument as a numbered list
surveys the history of the argument
checks.explanation: Stage 1 argues that something fitting a key description exists; Stage 2 argues that anything fitting it must have attributes such as unity, eternity, omnipotence, omniscience, and perfect goodness.

checks.q: A step in the formal argument that begins “So, …” is most likely…
options: a premise needing independent defence
an objection
an inference drawn from earlier steps
a definition
checks.explanation: “So” is an inference indicator. Such steps need only a valid link to earlier steps; the independent defence belongs to the premises.

checks.q: What is the best first response to feeling overwhelmed by a fifty-step argument?
options: read all fifty steps repeatedly until they stick
skip the formal statement entirely
start with the objections section instead
recall that it recaps the informal pages, and break it into blocks of steps that do one job each
checks.explanation: The formal statement introduces nothing new. Reading it as four or five functional blocks, each with a job, makes a long argument tractable.

argument.name: How to read an argument
argument.overview:
This module has no argument of its own to defend — Feser’s book supplies those. What it offers instead is a worked demonstration of the skill you will use in every chapter: taking reasoning written in ordinary prose and laying it out as numbered steps you can inspect one at a time.

We do it twice. **Stage A** takes a short, completely ordinary argument about a wet street and reconstructs it, so you can see the machinery — premise, hidden premise, inference, conclusion — on something with no philosophical weight attached.

**Stage B** then does the same job on the Aristotelian proof of chapter 1, compressed from Feser’s fifty steps to ten. This is a *simplified* version made for beginners: it keeps the logical spine and drops the derivation of the individual divine attributes, which occupies steps 15–47 of the real thing. Do not quote it as Feser’s argument. Use it as a map you can hold in your head, so that when you meet the full fifty steps on pages 35–37 you already know the shape of the country.

Each step below carries four things: **why** the step should be accepted, an **example** that makes it concrete, the most natural **challenge** to that step, and the **answer** the book gives. Read them in that order. When you get to the real chapters, do exactly this for the steps that carry weight — usually the premises, rarely the inferences.

stages.title: Stage A — An everyday argument, reconstructed
stages.gist: A three-sentence argument about wet streets, pulled apart into premises, a hidden premise, an inference and a conclusion, to show the technique on something harmless.

stages.title: Stage B — The Aristotelian proof in ten steps
stages.gist: A beginner’s compression of chapter 1: from the fact of change, through the analysis of change as actualization of a potential and the impossibility of an infinite hierarchical regress, to a purely actual actualizer.

steps.why: This is an observation — something the arguer takes you to be able to check for yourself. Arguments have to start somewhere, and the usual starting points are observations, definitions, or claims the audience already accepts.
steps.example: You look out the window and see the pavement gleaming.
steps.challenge: Perhaps it only looks wet — a trick of the light, or a fresh coat of sealant.
steps.answer: Fair, and the way to settle it is to go and touch the street. Notice how quickly a disputed premise turns into a concrete test. Philosophical premises are rarely settled this easily, but the move is the same: ask what would show it false.

steps.text: Hidden premise: whenever the street is wet, it has rained.
steps.why: This premise is never stated in the original sentence (‘The street is wet, so it must have rained’), but the argument collapses without it. Finding the unstated assumption is the single most useful habit in reading argumentative prose.
steps.example: The arguer says ‘the street is wet, so it rained’ and would be baffled if you asked what connects the two — precisely because he is assuming this link without noticing.
steps.challenge: This premise is false: streets get wet from street cleaners, burst mains, sprinklers, and hoses.
steps.answer: Exactly right, and that is the argument’s real weakness — which we found only by digging the premise out. This is what makes the technique worth learning: the flaw was invisible while the assumption stayed buried.

steps.why: Follows from 1 and 2 by a valid form: if all Ws are Rs, and this is a W, then this is an R. The inference itself is beyond reproach.
steps.example: Compare: all whales are mammals; this is a whale; so this is a mammal. Same shape, same validity.
steps.challenge: But the conclusion might still be false!
steps.answer: Yes — and that is precisely the difference between validity and soundness. The reasoning is valid; the argument is unsound, because premise 2 is false. A valid argument transmits truth, but it cannot manufacture it.

steps.text: Therefore the street’s being wet is evidence of rain — but only weak evidence, because premise 2 is false as stated.
steps.why: Having found the false premise, we can repair rather than discard: replace ‘whenever’ with ‘usually’, and the argument becomes a decent inductive one rather than a bad deductive one.
steps.example: ‘The street is wet, and rain is by far the commonest cause of that around here, so it probably rained.’ Weaker conclusion, much better argument.
steps.challenge: Isn’t this just nitpicking about a trivial example?
steps.answer: The example is trivial on purpose. The technique is not. Every argument in Feser’s book can be handled exactly this way, and the flaw in a bad objection is almost always a premise the objector never noticed he was using.

steps.why: Feser offers three layers of support. Our senses show it constantly — coffee cools, leaves fall, puddles spread, flies die. Even if the senses were entirely deceiving us, we would still be having one experience after another, which is itself change. And anyone arguing that change is an illusion must move through the steps of his argument, which is a change; so the denial cannot be coherently made.
steps.example: The four kinds of change on the chapter’s first page: qualitative (coffee cooling), local (a leaf falling), quantitative (a puddle growing), substantial (a living fly becoming dead matter).
steps.challenge: Parmenides argued that change is impossible: the coldness of the coffee was nothing before and is something after, and nothing comes from nothing.
steps.answer: Aristotle’s reply is that the coldness was not nothing beforehand — it was there potentially. The coffee has a potential to grow cold and no potential to become chicken soup, and that difference shows potentiality is a real feature of it, not sheer nothingness.

steps.text: Change is the actualization of a potential: something that was able to be a certain way comes to be that way.
steps.why: This is not a dictionary definition but Aristotle’s analysis, adopted because it dissolves Parmenides’ problem. If potentials are real, change involves no coming-from-nothing; it is the reduction of an already-real capacity to actuality.
steps.example: Water in the freezer is actually liquid and potentially solid. Freezing actualizes that potential. It was never potentially a violin.
steps.challenge: ‘Potentiality’ sounds like a word that explains nothing — a dormitive-virtue dodge.
steps.answer: Potentials discriminate, and a concept that rules things out is not empty. Feser addresses this in chapter 6 against Cottingham: explanations in terms of potentiality may be minimally informative, but minimally informative is not uninformative.

steps.text: Nothing can actualize its own potential: any potential that gets actualized is actualized by something already actual. (This is the principle of causality.)
steps.why: A merely potential F cannot do anything precisely because it is merely potential, and only what is actual can act. Potential coldness chills nothing; actual coldness — the air, the ice — does the chilling. Note carefully what this principle does *not* say: it does not say everything has a cause.
steps.example: The coffee’s not-yet-existing coldness cannot reach out and cool the coffee. Something already cold has to do it.
steps.challenge: Quantum mechanics describes events with no determining cause, such as radioactive decay.
steps.answer: Chapter 1 devotes a long section to this. Quantum physics at most shows that some events lack deterministic causes; it does not show that potentials actualize themselves without anything actual. On any interpretation there is an actual quantum system with actual properties doing the work.

steps.text: So whenever something changes, something already actual is actualizing it.
steps.why: Follows immediately from 6 and 7. Nothing new is being claimed; the two previous steps are simply being put together.
steps.example: The fly dies because the swatter strikes; the swatter moves because your wrist flicks; your wrist flicks because motor neurons fire.
steps.challenge: Doesn’t this mean whatever causes a change must itself be changing?
steps.answer: No, and Feser flags this explicitly. The claim is conditional: *if* the changer is itself being changed, then that change needs a changer too. He does not assert, and does not believe, that every cause of change is changing.

steps.text: A thing does not merely need a cause of how it got here. Its existing at this very moment is itself the actualization of a potential, and so needs an actualizer here and now.
steps.why: This is the step that turns the argument from a story about the past into an argument about the present, and it is the one beginners most often skate past. The water in your coffee exists now only because certain potentials of hydrogen and oxygen are being actualized as water rather than as separate gases; the atoms exist only because certain potentials of subatomic particles are being actualized in this arrangement.
steps.example: Asking what keeps the water in existence right now — not what combined the hydrogen and oxygen years ago, and not what might separate them later.
steps.challenge: Why not say things simply keep existing on their own once they exist? (The thesis of existential inertia.)
steps.answer: Feser’s reply is that a contingent thing’s existing is not a neutral default but the ongoing actualization of a potential — its essence being conjoined with existence, in chapter 4’s language. What would do the conjoining, on the inertia view, is left unexplained; and the chemical and atomic facts show that at every level some potential is being actualized rather than another.

steps.text: That actualizer, if it is itself having its own potentials actualized, needs an actualizer of its own — and so we have a series.
steps.why: The reasoning of steps 7 and 9 applies to the actualizer just as much as to the thing actualized. Either the actualizer is itself a mixture of actuality and potentiality, and the question recurs, or it is not.
steps.example: The water exists because of what is happening with the atoms; the atoms because of what is happening with the subatomic particles; and so on downward.
steps.challenge: Isn’t this just the endless ‘why?’ of a small child?
steps.answer: The child’s questions run along a timeline and can reasonably stop at ‘that’s just how it started’. These questions run downward through levels of present dependence, where stopping at an unexplained level does not answer but cancels the explanation, as the shelf example in chapter 5 shows.

steps.text: This is a hierarchical (per se) series, not a linear (per accidens) one: every member except the first has its power only by deriving it from something else at the moment it acts.
steps.why: The defining mark is derivative, instrumental power. The desk has no power of its own to hold up a cup; remove the floor and both fall. Contrast a line of ancestors or a switched-on air conditioner, whose members keep their power once they have it.
steps.example: Cup, desk, floor, foundation, earth — all at one instant, each borrowing from the next.
steps.challenge: Relativity shows there is no absolute simultaneity, so a series of simultaneous causes is a confused notion.
steps.answer: Feser is careful that simultaneity is a teaching aid, not the definition. What makes a series hierarchical is the derivative character of the later members, not their sharing a moment on the clock. The objection therefore hits the illustration and not the argument.

steps.text: A hierarchical series cannot go on forever. Its members are all borrowers, and no number of borrowers produces what none of them has.
steps.why: This is the load-bearing premise of the whole proof, and Feser argues for it with images rather than assertion: a paintbrush cannot move itself, and would not move itself if its handle were infinitely long; an infinite stack of desks holds up a cup exactly as well as one desk does, which is to say not at all.
steps.example: An infinitely long train of boxcars with no locomotive moves nowhere.
steps.challenge: Why can’t the series be infinite? Every member has a predecessor, so every member is accounted for.
steps.answer: That reply works for linear series, where each member has power of its own once acted upon, and Feser grants it there — he even grants a beginningless universe for the sake of argument. It fails for hierarchical series precisely because the members have no power of their own to account for.

steps.text: So the series terminates in something that can actualize without itself being actualized — something with no potentials needing actualization at all. Call it purely actual.
steps.why: Follows from 10, 11 and 12. Note what ‘first’ means here: not earliest in time, but non-derivative — having the power built in rather than borrowed.
steps.example: Not a starting gun at the Big Bang, but the painter at the end of the brush handle, however long the handle.
steps.challenge: Why not stop at something less than that — a fundamental particle, a quantum field, the laws of physics?
steps.answer: Because any such candidate is a mixture of actuality and potentiality: it could have been otherwise, it has parts, it is arranged one way rather than another. Anything with unactualized potentials is a borrower, and the series does not stop at a borrower. Feser makes this point against Krauss in chapter 7: layers of laws are themselves a hierarchical series.

steps.text: There exists a purely actual actualizer — and chapter 1 then argues that anything purely actual must be unique, immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, fully good, omnipotent and omniscient: in other words, God.
steps.why: The derivation of the attributes occupies steps 15–47 of Feser’s formal statement and follows one repeating pattern: attribute X would require an unactualized potential; a purely actual thing has none; therefore not-X. Uniqueness comes separately, from the argument that two purely actual things could not be differentiated.
steps.example: Immutability: to change is to have a potential actualized, and there are none, so it cannot change. Eternity: existing in time would involve change, so it is outside time.
steps.challenge: Even granting a purely actual actualizer, why call it God rather than some impersonal cosmic fact?
steps.answer: This is exactly what Stage 2 of each chapter exists to answer, and it is the objection you will meet most often in conversation. The claim is not that we decide to call it God, but that the same metaphysics that gets us to pure actuality also delivers intellect, will, omnipotence, omniscience and perfect goodness. Anyone who resists should be asked which of those derivations he rejects, and why.

keyTerms.definition: An a priori claim can be known independently of particular experience, by reasoning alone; an a posteriori claim can only be known through experience. The distinction concerns how a claim is known, not whether it is certain.
keyTerms.example: That no bachelor is married is known a priori; that there are seven continents is known a posteriori.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘from what is prior’ and ‘from what is later’; standard in Scholastic logic and made famous by Kant.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Necessary and contingent. A priori is about how we know a thing; necessary is about how the thing itself must be. Some philosophers argue there are necessary truths known a posteriori.

keyTerms.definition: Something real that is not located in space or time, cannot be perceived by the senses, and does not enter into causal interactions. Universals, propositions, numbers and possible worlds are the standard examples.
keyTerms.example: The number 2 is an abstract object; the numeral ‘2’ written on a page is a concrete mark that labels it.
keyTerms.origin: From Latin abstrahere, ‘to draw away’ — we abstract from the individual features of concrete things.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Something imaginary or vague. ‘Abstract’ in philosophy means non-spatial and non-causal, not unreal or fuzzy.

keyTerms.definition: The mental act of considering what is common to many things while ignoring the features that individuate them. It is how the intellect grasps universals from particular experience.
keyTerms.example: Seeing many triangles of different sizes and materials and forming the concept of triangularity, leaving out wood, metal, green and orange.
keyTerms.origin: Latin abstrahere, ‘to draw away from’; central to Aristotelian and Thomistic accounts of how the intellect works.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Generalization in the inductive sense. Abstraction isolates a nature; induction estimates how often something holds.

keyTerms.definition: A feature that exists only in something else rather than in its own right — a colour, a size, a position, a mood. Contrasted with substance, which exists in its own right.
keyTerms.example: The brownness of a dog, its weight of forty pounds, its being on the rug. None of these goes for a walk by itself.
keyTerms.origin: Latin accidens, ‘what happens to’ something; Aristotle’s Categories.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The everyday sense of ‘accident’ as a mishap. A philosophical accident may be entirely intended — the paint on a painted wall is an accident of the wall.

keyTerms.definition: A form that modifies an already existing substance rather than making it the kind of thing it is. It answers the question ‘how is this thing?’, not ‘what is it?’
keyTerms.example: The whiteness of a white house; the house is already a house without it.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic vocabulary developing Aristotle’s hylomorphism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Substantial form, which makes a thing the kind of thing it is in the first place.

keyTerms.definition: The way a thing really is at a given moment — its realized state, as opposed to what it merely could be. In the tradition, only what is actual can do anything.
keyTerms.example: The coffee’s actual heat right now; your actual reading of this sentence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin actus, translating Greek energeia / entelecheia; Aristotle’s Physics and Metaphysics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Existence. Everything actual exists, but ‘actuality’ picks out the realized-versus-potential contrast, while ‘existence’ contrasts with essence.

keyTerms.definition: The making-actual of something that was previously only potential. Feser defines change itself as the actualization of a potential, and a cause as whatever does the actualizing.
keyTerms.example: The cold air actualizes the coffee’s potential to be cold; the desk actualizes the cup’s potential to be three feet off the floor.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian; the Latin reductio de potentia ad actum, ‘reduction from potency to act’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Creation out of nothing. Actualization presupposes something with the potential; creation ex nihilo does not.

keyTerms.definition: The fallacy of attacking the person making an argument instead of the argument itself, as if the arguer’s character or motives settled whether the reasoning works.
keyTerms.example: ‘You only believe that because you were raised religious.’ True or false, it says nothing about whether the premises are true and the inference valid.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘to the man’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Legitimate challenges to testimony. Questioning whether a witness is reliable can be fair; questioning whether an argument is valid by reference to who gave it is not.

keyTerms.definition: The principle that the way a thing acts follows from what it is: a thing’s characteristic activities cannot go beyond its nature. One of three background principles Feser sets out at the start of chapter 6.
keyTerms.example: Plants take in nutrients, grow and reproduce while stones do not, because of what each is. A stone that used language would not be a stone.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘action follows being’; a Scholastic maxim used heavily by Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The principle of proportionate causality, which is the parallel claim about efficient causes — that an effect cannot exceed its total cause.

keyTerms.definition: A use of a word in related but not identical senses across two cases — the middle option between univocal and equivocal use. Classical theists hold that terms applied to God and to creatures are used analogically.
keyTerms.example: ‘This wine is good’ and ‘George is a good man’ — different but related senses of ‘good’.
keyTerms.origin: Greek analogia, ‘proportion’; developed by Aquinas into a theory of religious language.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphorical. Analogical predication is literal; ‘God is a rock’ is metaphor, ‘God is good’ is analogy.

keyTerms.definition: Analogical usage in which a term applies primarily to one thing and secondarily to others because of their relation to it — as cause, sign, or effect.
keyTerms.example: A person is healthy; a diet is called healthy because it causes health; a complexion is called healthy because it signifies health.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic; Latin analogia attributionis.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Analogy of proper proportionality, where the relation is one of matching proportions rather than reference to one primary case.

keyTerms.definition: The thesis that ‘being’, ‘existence’ and ‘real’ are themselves used analogically rather than univocally, because different kinds of thing exist in different ways.
keyTerms.example: A stone is real and the stone’s colour is real, but a colour exists only in something else, so the two are not real in the same sense.
keyTerms.origin: Latin analogia entis; a hallmark of Thomistic metaphysics, introduced in chapter 2 and developed in chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Analogy as a method of argument (arguing from similar cases). The analogy of being is a claim about how words signify, not an inference pattern.

keyTerms.definition: Analogical usage in which a term applies to two things because of a similarity of proportions: A is to its nature as B is to its nature.
keyTerms.example: As sharpness is to a knife, so justice is to a person — each is the excellence proper to that kind of thing.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic; Latin analogia proportionalitatis propriae.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphorical proportionality, as in ‘the lion is the king of beasts’, which is not a literal use.

keyTerms.definition: A set of statements (premises) offered as reasons for accepting another statement (the conclusion). In philosophy an argument is a structure to be inspected, not a quarrel.
keyTerms.example: All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal.
keyTerms.origin: Latin argumentum, ‘evidence, proof’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An explanation. An argument tries to show that something is true; an explanation assumes it is true and says why.

keyTerms.definition: The fallacy of assuming in the premises the very thing the argument is supposed to prove, so that the argument has no power to convince anyone not already persuaded.
keyTerms.example: ‘The book is reliable because it says so, and what it says is true because the book is reliable.’
keyTerms.origin: Latin petitio principii, ‘assuming the starting point’; the English phrase is a translation of Aristotle’s ‘asking for the initial thing’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The colloquial ‘begs the question’ meaning ‘invites the question’. That is a different and much weaker usage.

keyTerms.definition: A fact that has no explanation at all, not merely one we have not discovered. To accept brute facts is to deny the principle of sufficient reason.
keyTerms.example: Bertrand Russell’s reply that the universe is simply there and that is all — no explanation, in principle.
keyTerms.origin: Modern analytic philosophy; the position is associated with Russell and J. L. Mackie.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An unexplained fact. An unsolved murder is unexplained but not brute; the claim of bruteness is that there is nothing to find.

keyTerms.definition: In Feser’s central sense, whatever actualizes a potential. Note that this includes causes operating here and now to sustain a thing, not only causes that got something started in the past.
keyTerms.example: The floor is a cause of the desk’s holding up the cup at this very moment.
keyTerms.origin: Latin causa, translating Greek aitia, ‘that which is responsible for’; broader than the modern sense.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Efficient cause only. In Aristotle’s scheme material, formal and final causes are also causes, so ‘cause’ is wider than ‘what brought it about’.

keyTerms.definition: The actualization of a potential. Aristotle’s analysis answers Parmenides’ claim that change would require something to come from nothing.
keyTerms.example: Coffee cooling (qualitative), a leaf falling (local), a puddle spreading (quantitative), a fly dying (substantial).
keyTerms.origin: Greek kinēsis, often translated ‘motion’, but covering all four kinds of change, not just movement through space.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Motion in the modern sense of change of place. Aristotelian ‘motion’ is far broader.

keyTerms.definition: The traditional conception of God as pure actuality, absolutely simple, immutable, eternal, necessary, omnipotent, omniscient and perfectly good — the source of the existence of everything else rather than one being among others.
keyTerms.example: The God of Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Maimonides, Avicenna, Anselm and Aquinas — and the God Feser’s five proofs conclude to.
keyTerms.origin: A modern label for the mainstream of Western philosophical theology; divine simplicity is regarded as its core.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Theistic personalism, which treats God as the unique member of a genus of persons, immensely powerful but still composite.

keyTerms.definition: Made up of parts — whether physical parts or metaphysical ones such as form and matter, essence and existence, substance and accidents, act and potency. Composites depend on their parts and on whatever unites them.
keyTerms.example: A chair, which exists only if its legs, frame and seat exist and are arranged chairwise at this moment.
keyTerms.origin: Latin compositus, ‘put together’; central to the Neo-Platonic proof of chapter 2.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Complicated. A thing can be metaphysically composite while being behaviourally very simple, such as an electron.

keyTerms.definition: The view that universals are real but exist only as concepts in human minds. It is one of the three standard positions on universals that chapter 3 examines.
keyTerms.example: Holding that triangularity exists only when someone forms the general idea of a triangle.
keyTerms.origin: Medieval debates over universals, associated with Abelard and later with Locke.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Nominalism, which denies universals altogether and says only the general word exists. Conceptualism allows a general idea; nominalism allows only a general name.

keyTerms.definition: The statement an argument is trying to establish; the claim the premises are offered in support of.
keyTerms.example: In ‘All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; so Socrates is mortal’, the conclusion is that Socrates is mortal.
keyTerms.origin: Latin conclusio, ‘a closing’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A summary. A conclusion is supported by reasons; a summary merely restates.

keyTerms.definition: An object located in space and time that can stand in causal relations — the opposite of an abstract object.
keyTerms.example: This billiard ball, this dog, this galaxy.
keyTerms.origin: Latin concretus, ‘grown together’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Material object. Classical theists regard angels and human souls as concrete yet immaterial.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that is actualizing something’s potential at the very moment that thing exists or acts, as opposed to a cause that acted earlier. The regress of concurrent actualizers is what chapter 1’s argument traces.
keyTerms.example: Whatever is sustaining the water’s molecular arrangement right now, as against whatever combined the hydrogen and oxygen years ago.
keyTerms.origin: ‘Concurrent’ in the sense of running together; the notion is Scholastic, connected to divine concurrence.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A simultaneous cause. Concurrence is about dependence, not merely about sharing a moment on the clock.

keyTerms.definition: Existing, but able not to have existed; true, but able to have been otherwise. Contingent things come into being and pass away and require something outside themselves to account for their existence.
keyTerms.example: You, the moon, lions — all exist, and all might not have.
keyTerms.origin: Latin contingere, ‘to happen, to befall’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Dependent, in the everyday sense of ‘conditional on’. Philosophically the core meaning is ‘could have failed to be’, from which dependence follows.

keyTerms.definition: Any argument that reasons from some general feature of the world — change, causation, contingency, composition — to a first cause or necessary being. Four of Feser’s five proofs are cosmological in this broad sense.
keyTerms.example: Aquinas’ First Way, Leibniz’s argument from contingency, and Feser’s Aristotelian and Thomistic proofs.
keyTerms.origin: Greek kosmos, ‘world, order’; the label is Kant’s.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The ontological argument, which reasons from the concept of God alone with no premise about the world; and the design argument, which reasons from apparent purpose or fine-tuning.

keyTerms.definition: A single case that shows a general claim to be false, or that an argument form is invalid. Producing one is among the most efficient ways to attack a premise.
keyTerms.example: ‘All swans are white’ is refuted by one black swan.
keyTerms.origin: Standard logical vocabulary.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A mere exception that has been allowed for. A qualified claim (‘all swans in Europe before 1697’) is not touched by a counterexample outside its scope.

keyTerms.definition: Reasoning in which the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises: if the premises are true, the conclusion cannot be false. Feser presents his proofs as deductive.
keyTerms.example: All squares are rectangles; this is a square; therefore this is a rectangle.
keyTerms.origin: Latin deducere, ‘to lead down from’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Induction, in which true premises make the conclusion probable but not guaranteed.

keyTerms.definition: A deductive argument whose conclusion follows necessarily from premises that are themselves certain. This is the strong claim Feser makes for his proofs — not that God is probable, but that God follows.
keyTerms.example: A geometrical proof: given the axioms, the theorem is not likely but necessary.
keyTerms.origin: Latin demonstratio, translating Aristotle’s apodeixis in the Posterior Analytics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Proof in the loose sense of ‘strong evidence’. A demonstration claims necessity, not weight of evidence.

keyTerms.definition: An argument from apparent purpose, order or fine-tuning in nature to a designer. Usually framed as an inference to the best explanation and therefore probabilistic.
keyTerms.example: Paley’s watch on the heath; contemporary fine-tuning arguments.
keyTerms.origin: Also called the teleological argument, from Greek telos, ‘end, goal’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Feser’s five proofs, none of which is a design argument. He regards the difference as important: his arguments claim demonstration, not probability.

keyTerms.definition: A distinction that reflects only our way of thinking or speaking about a thing, with nothing in the thing itself corresponding to it. Contrasted with a real distinction.
keyTerms.example: ‘Bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’ pick out exactly the same reality.
keyTerms.origin: Latin distinctio rationis; standard Scholastic vocabulary.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A real distinction, which tracks a difference in mind-independent reality. Chapter 4 argues that essence and existence differ really, not merely in reason.

keyTerms.definition: The characteristics classical theism ascribes to God — unity, simplicity, immutability, immateriality, incorporeality, eternity, necessity, omnipotence, omniscience, perfect goodness, will, love, incomprehensibility.
keyTerms.example: Steps 15–47 of chapter 1’s formal argument derive most of these from pure actuality.
keyTerms.origin: A standing topic of philosophical theology; chapter 6 treats it systematically.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Properties in the ordinary sense. Given divine simplicity, the attributes are not distinct components of God but one reality grasped under several concepts.

keyTerms.definition: The doctrine that the world could not exist even for an instant unless God were continually sustaining it in being. It is the theological counterpart of the here-and-now causal series.
keyTerms.example: Not God winding a clock and walking away, but God keeping the clock in existence at every tick.
keyTerms.origin: Latin conservatio; defended in the second half of chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Deism, which holds that God started things and then left them to run. Conservation denies exactly that.

keyTerms.definition: What brings something about or produces a change in it — the closest of Aristotle’s four causes to the modern everyday meaning of ‘cause’.
keyTerms.example: The carpenter, in relation to the chair; the cold air, in relation to the cooled coffee.
keyTerms.origin: Latin causa efficiens, translating Aristotle’s ‘that from which the change originates’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Final cause, which is what something is for. Modern usage tends to collapse all four causes into the efficient one.

keyTerms.definition: The branch of philosophy concerned with knowledge: what it is, how we get it, when a belief is justified, and what the limits of knowing are.
keyTerms.example: Asking whether we can trust the senses, or what makes a scientific theory well confirmed.
keyTerms.origin: Greek epistēmē, ‘knowledge’, plus logos, ‘account’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphysics, which asks what reality is like rather than how we know it. Many disputes in this book turn on keeping the two apart.

keyTerms.definition: A use of the same word in two completely different and unrelated senses, sharing nothing but the spelling or the sound.
keyTerms.example: The bat that flew around the attic and the bat you swung at it.
keyTerms.origin: Latin aequivocus, ‘called by the same name’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Analogical use, where the senses differ but are genuinely related. Treating God-talk as equivocal would make theology meaningless.

keyTerms.definition: What a thing is — the nature that makes it the kind of thing it is, as opposed to the fact that it exists.
keyTerms.example: A triangle’s essence is being a closed three-sided plane figure; a human being’s, on the traditional definition, is being a rational animal.
keyTerms.origin: Latin essentia, coined to translate Greek to ti ēn einai, ‘the what-it-is-to-be’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The gist or the important part, in the loose everyday sense. Philosophically, essence is a thing’s defining nature, not its most striking feature.

keyTerms.definition: In classical theism, existence outside of time altogether, not merely endless duration within time. Anything in time would be subject to change, and pure actuality cannot change.
keyTerms.example: Not a being who has already lasted forever and will go on lasting, but one for whom there is no before and after at all.
keyTerms.origin: Latin aeternitas; Boethius’ classic formula describes it as the complete possession of unending life all at once.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Everlastingness (sempiternity), which is duration without end but still within time.

keyTerms.definition: The fact that a thing actually is, as opposed to what it is. In contingent things, really distinct from essence; in God, identical with it.
keyTerms.example: You can fully understand what a unicorn is while knowing that there are none; the second question is about existence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin existere, ‘to stand forth’; the Scholastic term is esse, ‘to be’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being a property among a thing’s properties. On the Thomistic account existence is not one attribute on a list but the actuality of the whole essence.

keyTerms.definition: The thesis that once a thing exists it simply continues to exist unless something destroys it, so that no sustaining cause is needed. It is the main rival to divine conservation.
keyTerms.example: Claiming that the water in a glass needs no cause to keep existing from moment to moment, only a cause to have started existing.
keyTerms.origin: A modern coinage by analogy with Newtonian inertia; Feser has written on it at length.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Newtonian inertia in physics, which concerns motion rather than existence. The verbal parallel is what makes the thesis sound more established than it is.

keyTerms.definition: A supposed explanation in which A is explained by B while B is explained by A, so that nothing has actually been explained.
keyTerms.example: Saying the chair’s parts are held together by the chair, when the chair exists only because the parts are already held together.
keyTerms.origin: A species of the fallacy of begging the question, applied to explanations rather than arguments.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A legitimate feedback loop in nature, where two things influence each other over time. The vicious circle is a simultaneous dependence of each on the other.

keyTerms.definition: In this context, assent to something on the authority of a revelation, as opposed to assent on the basis of unaided reasoning. Feser’s project deliberately sets faith aside.
keyTerms.example: Believing a doctrine because one takes it to have been revealed in Scripture rather than because one has argued to it.
keyTerms.origin: Latin fides, ‘trust’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Belief without evidence, or wishful thinking. That popular definition would make natural theology incoherent from the start, which is one reason Feser is careful to distinguish the two sources.

keyTerms.definition: A pattern of reasoning that fails — either because the conclusion does not follow from the premises (a formal fallacy) or because of some defect in how the argument is framed or supported (an informal fallacy).
keyTerms.example: Affirming the consequent: ‘If it rained, the street is wet; the street is wet; so it rained.’
keyTerms.origin: Latin fallacia, ‘deceit’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A false claim. An argument can be fallacious with a true conclusion, and non-fallacious with a false one.

keyTerms.definition: Applying a general rule to a case it was never meant to cover, ignoring features of that case that make it an exception.
keyTerms.example: ‘Cutting people with knives is wrong, so surgeons act wrongly.’
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s Sophistical Refutations; Latin fallacia accidentis.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The fallacy of composition, which moves from parts to whole. The fallacy of accident moves from a general rule to a special case.

keyTerms.definition: Inferring that what is true of the parts must be true of the whole. Some part-to-whole inferences are perfectly good; the fallacy lies in assuming they always are.
keyTerms.example: ‘Every brick is light, so the wall is light.’ Compare the valid ‘every brick is red, so the wall is red.’
keyTerms.origin: Classical logic; the standard name in English textbooks.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The fallacy of division, which runs the other way — from whole to parts. Feser argues in chapter 7 that critics who press this charge often commit it themselves.

keyTerms.definition: What something is for, or what it naturally tends toward — the ‘that for the sake of which’ among Aristotle’s four causes.
keyTerms.example: Being sat on, in the case of a chair; pumping blood, in the case of a heart.
keyTerms.origin: Latin causa finalis, from finis, ‘end, goal’; Greek telos.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conscious purpose. Aristotelian final causality is present in unconscious nature too — acorns tend toward oaks without intending to.

keyTerms.definition: Aquinas’ five brief arguments for God’s existence in the Summa Theologiae: from motion, from causality, from contingency, from degrees of perfection, and from finality.
keyTerms.example: The First Way argues from motion to an Unmoved Mover.
keyTerms.origin: Latin quinque viae, Summa Theologiae I, q. 2, a. 3.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Feser’s Five Proofs. He states at the very opening of the book that it is not about the Five Ways; only two of his five proofs are found in Aquinas.

keyTerms.definition: The organizing pattern or structure that makes a thing be the kind of thing it is, as opposed to the matter it is made of.
keyTerms.example: The same bronze can have the form of a statue or the form of a doorstop.
keyTerms.origin: Latin forma, translating Greek morphē or eidos.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Shape. Shape is one kind of form, but form in general includes the whole organization and powers of a thing, not just its outline.

keyTerms.definition: In Plato, a perfect, unchanging, mind-independent pattern existing in a realm of its own, which individual things imperfectly copy or participate in.
keyTerms.example: The Form of the Triangle, of which every drawn triangle is an imperfect instance.
keyTerms.origin: Plato’s dialogues, especially the Republic and Phaedo.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Aristotelian form, which exists in things rather than in a separate realm. Chapter 3 accepts the reality of the patterns but relocates them into a divine intellect.

keyTerms.definition: A thing’s form or structure considered as an answer to ‘why is it as it is?’ — one of Aristotle’s four causes.
keyTerms.example: The chair-structure of an arrangement of wood, which is why it is a chair rather than a pile.
keyTerms.origin: Latin causa formalis.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Efficient cause. The carpenter is the efficient cause of the chair; the chair-structure is its formal cause.

keyTerms.definition: The section of each proof chapter where Feser lays the argument out as an explicit numbered series of steps, so its logical structure is visible.
keyTerms.example: Chapter 1’s fifty-step statement, which recaps the informal pages that precede it.
keyTerms.origin: Feser’s own term, explained in the Introduction; the style is that of contemporary analytic philosophy.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Formal logic. The statement is numbered and structured, but not symbolic.

keyTerms.definition: The three ways the principle of proportionate causality says what is in an effect can be in its total cause: formally (the cause has the very same feature), virtually (it has the power to produce it), or eminently (it has a higher power that can bring it about).
keyTerms.example: Giving you $20 from my wallet (formally), by wire from my account (virtually), or by having access to a press that prints the bill (eminently).
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic; Latin formaliter, virtualiter, eminenter.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The everyday sense of ‘virtually’ as ‘almost’. Here it means ‘in the mode of a power’.

keyTerms.definition: Aristotle’s four ways of answering ‘why?’ about a thing: material (what it is made of), formal (what it is), efficient (what brought it about) and final (what it is for).
keyTerms.example: A chair: wood; chair-structure; the carpenter; being sat on.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle, Physics II; Greek aitiai.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Four competing explanations. They are complementary answers to different questions, not rivals.

keyTerms.definition: A broader class under which more specific kinds fall. Together with the specific difference, it forms the traditional structure of a definition.
keyTerms.example: Animal is the genus under which the species human being falls.
