objections.objection: Everything needs an explanation — except your favoured thing, which conveniently explains itself. That is textbook special pleading, and no amount of Latin makes it respectable.
objections.reply:
Special pleading is exempting a favoured case *without a principled reason*. The whole content of these arguments is the principled reason.

The rule is not ‘everything needs a cause’. It is that things need causes *because of a specific feature they have*: potentiality needing actualization, parts needing to be united, essence needing to be conjoined with existence, contingency needing an explanation beyond itself. The terminus of each argument is characterized precisely by lacking that feature. It is not exempted from the rule; it does not satisfy the rule's antecedent.

Compare: ‘every borrower must get the money from someone’ is a fine rule, and it does not make an exception for the person who owns the money. He is not a borrower.
objections.pushback: If the objector says ‘you just assert that God lacks the feature’, he has spotted the real issue and you should concede it: it is not asserted, it is argued, and the argument is the fifty steps. Invite him to say which step manufactures the exemption. He will have to read the chapter — which is the best possible outcome.

objections.title: “I can’t even picture what you’re describing — doesn’t that mean it’s nonsense?”
objections.whoRaises: The honest beginner, including many sympathetic readers
objections.objection: Something outside time, with no parts, that doesn’t change, whose essence is its existence — I cannot form any mental image of that at all. If I cannot picture it, in what sense do I understand it?
objections.reply:
You are noticing something real, and the tradition noticed it first: this is why chapter 6 ascribes **incomprehensibility** to God. But imaginability is not the test of intelligibility, and this is worth getting clear about early.

You cannot picture the number seventeen, or the proposition that snow is white, or a thousand-sided polygon as distinct from a nine-hundred-and-ninety-nine-sided one. You understand all three perfectly well, and you can reason about them rigorously. The intellect grasps things the imagination cannot supply a picture for — that is precisely what distinguishes it from imagination.

What you can do with the divine attributes is exactly what you do with the chiliagon: follow the reasoning, hold the definition, draw the consequences, and notice that your inability to visualize has no bearing on whether the reasoning works.
objections.pushback: If the objector says ‘then you are talking about something you don’t understand’, distinguish two claims. We do not comprehend God exhaustively — the tradition insists on that. But we can know true things about him by valid argument from what we do understand, and those claims are literal, not metaphorical. That is what the doctrine of analogy is for.

objections.title: “Believing in God is like believing in Zeus — you’re an atheist about every god but one”
objections.whoRaises: Dawkins and the New Atheists; the ‘one god further’ line
objections.objection: You reject Zeus, Thor, Vishnu and several thousand others on perfectly good grounds. Consistency requires going one god further and rejecting yours too.
objections.reply:
The line trades entirely on the ambiguity this whole module has been trying to remove. Zeus is a very powerful being *inside* the universe — he has a body, a location, a history, moods, parents. Rejecting him is rejecting an item in the world’s inventory that turns out not to be there.

The God of classical theism is not that kind of candidate at all. He is not one more being among beings; he is pure actuality, that in virtue of which anything exists at all. So the two rejections would be doing completely different work: one is like concluding there is no undiscovered planet, the other like concluding there is no such thing as existence. The inference from the first to the second is not consistency; it is a change of subject.

Feser deals with the ‘one god further’ objection in chapter 7 (around pages 289–292) and argues that it rests on precisely this confusion.
objections.pushback: If the objector replies that this is just special pleading for one’s own god, point out that the distinction is not between my god and yours but between two *categories* — a being within the world and the source of the world’s being. A polytheist who upgraded Zeus to pure actuality would no longer be describing Zeus.

misconceptions.myth: ‘Natural theology’ means theology that studies nature, or a religion based on nature.
misconceptions.correction: It means what can be known about God by unaided reason, apart from revelation. Feser defines it that way in the Introduction. The contrast is with revealed theology, not with supernatural theology.

misconceptions.myth: A ‘valid’ argument is one with true premises.
misconceptions.correction: Validity is about form only: if the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true. ‘All cats are reptiles; Fido is a cat; so Fido is a reptile’ is perfectly valid and has two false premises. An argument that is valid *and* has true premises is called sound.

misconceptions.myth: ‘Everything has a cause’ is the first premise of the cosmological argument.
misconceptions.correction: No argument in this book uses it. The principle of causality says that no potential is actualized unless something already actual actualizes it. Almost every popular objection to these arguments attacks the version Feser never asserts.

misconceptions.myth: ‘First cause’ means the earliest cause, the one at the beginning of time.
misconceptions.correction: ‘First’ means non-derivative — having causal power built in rather than borrowed. The argument works even granting a beginningless universe, which Feser explicitly grants for the sake of argument. Picture a stack, not a timeline.

misconceptions.myth: The arguments depend on the universe having had a beginning, so Big Bang cosmology is what makes or breaks them.
misconceptions.correction: They are indifferent to it. Feser concedes an eternal universe or multiverse and argues that it would still require a cause sustaining it in being at every moment. Cosmology settles a question the arguments were not asking.

misconceptions.myth: A potential is just a logical possibility, so saying a thing has potentials says nothing.
misconceptions.correction: Potentials are specific and grounded in what a thing actually is. Coffee is potentially cold, potentially a stain, and not potentially chicken soup or a live chicken. A concept that rules things out is not empty.

It covers every kind of change: qualitative (cooling), local (falling), quantitative (growing) and substantial (a living thing becoming dead matter). The Unmoved Mover is unchanged, not merely stationary.

misconceptions.myth: Saying God is ‘simple’ means God is easy to understand.
misconceptions.correction: It means God has no parts of any kind — no matter and form, no essence distinct from existence, no accidents, no potentiality. Feser in fact holds God to be incomprehensible, and simplicity is a large part of the reason.

misconceptions.myth: Classical theists think God is impersonal, and theistic personalists think he is personal.
misconceptions.correction: Feser is explicit that this is not the difference. Most classical theists attribute intellect and will to God and regard him as personal. The dispute is over whether God falls under a genus — one kind of person among possible kinds — and is therefore composite.

misconceptions.myth: If we can only speak of God analogically, we do not really know what we are saying.
misconceptions.correction: Analogical predication is literal. ‘God is good’ is a true, literal claim, made with a word whose content is stretched rather than duplicated or abandoned. Feser objects specifically to the characterization of Aquinas’ view as making God-talk analogical rather than literal.

misconceptions.myth: This is a design argument: order in nature points to a designer.
misconceptions.correction: None of the five is a design argument, and Feser is careful about the difference. Design arguments infer to the best explanation of particular features of the world and yield probable conclusions. These arguments claim to demonstrate, from features anything whatever must have, that a certain cause exists.

misconceptions.myth: The numbered formal argument is the real argument; the chatty pages before it are just warm-up.
misconceptions.correction: Closer to the reverse. The informal statement carries the justification for the premises; the formal statement displays the structure. The numbered version introduces nothing new, which is exactly why a fifty-step list should not intimidate anyone who has read the pages before it.

misconceptions.myth: Philosophy is a matter of opinion, so nobody can be simply wrong.
misconceptions.correction: Arguments have premises that are true or false and inferences that are valid or invalid, and both can be checked. A great deal of chapter 7 consists of showing that specific, widely repeated objections are simply mistakes.

misconceptions.myth: An ‘abstract object’ is something vague, imaginary, or made up.
misconceptions.correction: It means something real that is not located in space or time and does not enter into causal relations — universals, propositions, numbers, possible worlds. The number 2 is not hazy; it is precise, and you cannot trip over it.

explain.tweet: Before reading Feser’s Five Proofs, learn six words. Potential = what a thing can become. Actual = how it is now. A per se causal series is a stack (cup on desk on floor), not a timeline. “First cause” means non-derivative, not earliest. That one fix answers half the objections.
explain.elevator: Feser’s book argues that God’s existence can be demonstrated by reason alone. But it uses a vocabulary most readers have never met: act and potency, essence and existence, hierarchical causal series, divine simplicity. This module teaches those words first, with everyday examples — cooling coffee, a cup on a desk, a $20 bill — so that when you open the book you are learning the arguments instead of decoding the terms.
explain.twoMinute:
Here is what nobody tells you before you open a book like this.

The arguments are not hard because the logic is hard. They are hard because about eight background ideas get introduced quickly and then used on every page afterwards. Miss one and the next forty pages feel like fog.

The biggest one is this. When most of us hear ‘what caused that?’, we think about the past — what got it started. Feser is almost always asking a different question: what is holding it in being *right now*? And he says there are two completely different kinds of causal chain. One runs backward through time, like a line of ancestors: your grandfather can be dead and the chain still stands. The other is stacked up at this instant, like a coffee cup held by a desk held by a floor held by a foundation held by the earth. In that second kind, every link is borrowing. The desk has no power of its own to keep a cup three feet up — take away the floor and both go down together.

And that is why he says the second kind must have a first member, while the first kind need not. ‘First’ doesn’t mean earliest. It means non-derivative — something with the power built in rather than borrowed. His best image: a paintbrush can’t move itself, and it still couldn’t if the handle were infinitely long. Length isn’t power.

Once you have that, look at what happens to the famous objections. ‘Maybe the universe is infinitely old’ — Feser grants that for the sake of argument; it’s about the other kind of chain. ‘Why can’t the regress be infinite?’ — for linear series, fine; for a stack of borrowers, adding borrowers never produces a lender. ‘Who made God?’ — the arguments never say everything has a cause; they say no *potential* gets actualized without something actual, and the thing they conclude to has no potentials.

The other big one is the word ‘God’. Most debates are two people arguing about different things. The God being defended here isn’t a very powerful being inside the universe. He’s pure actuality — no parts, no change, outside time, the reason anything exists at all. Half the standard objections are aimed at a target this book isn’t defending.

Learn those two things and you can read the book.
explain.eli12:
Imagine a coffee cup sitting on a desk.

Why is the cup up in the air instead of on the ground? The desk is holding it. What holds the desk? The floor. What holds the floor? The foundation of the house. What holds that? The earth.

Now here’s the interesting bit. The desk can’t hold anything up *by itself*. If the floor vanished, the desk would fall and the cup with it. Same for the floor: it only holds the desk because the foundation holds it. Every single one of them is borrowing the ability to hold things up from the thing below.

So ask yourself: could that chain go on forever? Imagine a million desks stacked up, all borrowing. A billion. Infinity of them. Does the cup stay up? No! Because none of them ever had the ability in the first place. They were all just passing along something that has to start somewhere.

Here’s another way to see it. A paintbrush can’t move itself. What if the handle were ten feet long? Still can’t. A mile long? Still can’t. Infinitely long? *Still can’t.* Making the handle longer never turns it into a painter. There has to be somebody holding it.

That is the main idea of this whole book. There are chains of things where everything is borrowing, and those chains have to start with something that isn’t borrowing — something that has the ability built in.

And one more thing. When people argue about God, they usually picture a really, really powerful person somewhere out in space. This book isn’t about that at all. It’s about whatever it is that makes anything exist in the first place — the thing at the bottom that isn’t borrowing from anything.
whiteboard: Draw a stick figure holding a paintbrush. Say: a brush can’t move itself. Now draw the handle running off the edge of the board. Say: make it infinitely long — still can’t move itself. Length isn’t power. That single picture is the heart of the book.

Draw two columns. Head the left ‘THEN’ and the right ‘NOW’. Under THEN, draw grandfather → father → son. Under NOW, draw a cup on a desk on a floor on the earth. Say: these are the two kinds of causal chain, and everything depends on telling them apart.

Under THEN write: ‘each keeps its power — grandfather can be dead.’ Under NOW write: ‘each borrows, right now — remove the floor and everything falls.’ Circle the NOW column. Say: the whole book is about this column.
Write ‘FIRST ≠ EARLIEST’ in large letters and box it. Say: first means the one with power built in. Not the starting gun. Draw an arrow from the box to the earth at the bottom of the NOW stack.

Draw a coffee cup and write beside it ACTUAL: hot, liquid, in a cup. Underneath write POTENTIAL: cold, spilled, a stain. Then write in a different colour: NOT chicken soup, NOT a chicken. Say: a potential is real but limited, which is why it isn’t the same as nothing.

Write the principle of causality in full: ‘No potential is actualized unless something already actual actualizes it.’ Then cross out, beneath it, ‘everything has a cause.’ Say: that second sentence is the one everybody attacks, and nobody in this book says it.

Draw two circles side by side. Label one ‘a very powerful being’ and put it inside a big box labelled ‘the universe’. Label the other ‘pure actuality’ and draw it outside the box, with arrows pointing into the box. Say: most arguments about God are two people pointing at different circles.

Write three sentences in a column: ‘Fido is a dog / Rover is a dog’ — label it UNIVOCAL. ‘A bat flew / I swung the bat’ — label it EQUIVOCAL. ‘Good wine / good man’ — label it ANALOGICAL. Say: God-talk is the third one, and it is literal, not metaphor.

Draw a bookshelf with a book on it, floating with nothing underneath. Write ‘brute fact?’ with an arrow to the shelf. Say: if the shelf has no tendency to stay up, it can’t give the book one. That’s the argument against stopping at an unexplained fact.

Finish by writing the four-part structure of every chapter: 1 informal Stage 1 / 2 informal Stage 2 / 3 formal numbered steps / 4 objections. Say: the numbered list is always a recap. You have already read it in prose.
explain.keyAnalogy: The infinitely long paintbrush. Use it the moment anyone says ‘why can’t the causes just go back forever?’ — and use it physically: hold an imaginary brush, then keep backing away as the handle grows. Ask at each stage, ‘has it started painting yet?’ The listener will laugh, and the laugh is the understanding arriving. Then make the point explicit: adding length adds more of something that has no power of its own, and no amount of that ever adds up to power. Finish by naming the target: this is why the age of the universe is irrelevant to the argument. A beginningless universe is just a very long handle.

persuade.coreInsight:
**The insight:** there are two kinds of causal chain, and almost everyone has only ever thought about one of them.

The kind we all know runs backward through time and each link keeps its power once it has it. Your grandfather caused your father, who caused you, and your grandfather can be long dead. You pressed a button, the air conditioner came on, and it goes on cooling after you leave the house. Asking whether such a chain has a beginning is a reasonable question with no obvious answer, which is why people who have only this picture in mind hear ‘first cause’ as ‘the event at the very start’.

The other kind is stacked up at this instant, and every link is borrowing. The cup is three feet up because the desk holds it; the desk holds it only because the floor holds the desk; the floor only because the foundation. Nothing in the stack has any power of its own. And that changes everything about the regress question: adding more borrowers never produces a lender, so this kind of chain must terminate in something with power built in — which is what ‘first’ means here, not ‘earliest’.

**Why it usually fails to click.** Two reasons, and both are about the listener’s mental picture rather than their intelligence. First, the word ‘cause’ carries three centuries of habit pointing at the past; every time your listener hears ‘cause’ they will picture a timeline, and the whole argument will sound like an argument about the Big Bang. Second, the examples that make the second kind vivid — cup, desk, floor — sound so trivial that people assume they must be missing something deep, when in fact the triviality is the point: it is a structure you can see on your own desk.

**What to do about it.** Do not argue. Build the picture. Put an object on a table and ask what is holding it up, and keep asking. Only when your listener has the stack in their head should you introduce the word ‘first’, and then define it immediately: not earliest, but non-derivative. If you introduce the conclusion before the picture, they will fit it into the timeline they already have, and you will spend the rest of the conversation talking past each other.

audiences.startingPoint: Believes that physics is steadily explaining everything that needs explaining, that appeals to God are always appeals to gaps, and that metaphysics is what people did before they had instruments.
audiences.approach: Concede more than they expect. Grant the Big Bang, grant an eternal or cyclic multiverse, grant that every gap you can name will eventually close. Then point out that you have granted all of that and the question has not been touched, because the question is not how things work but why anything is there to work at all. Use the layered-laws point from chapter 7: if law C holds because of law B, and B because of A, you have a hierarchical series, and stopping at A as a brute fact does not explain B and C but cancels the explanation — because if A has no tendency of its own, it has nothing to impart.
audiences.openingQuestion: Suppose physics finishes tomorrow — a complete final theory, every constant derived, no gaps. Would that tell us why there is a universe for the theory to be about?
audiences.avoid: Never cite a scientific mystery as evidence. The moment you say ‘science can’t explain consciousness / the fine-tuning / the origin of life’, you have turned your argument into exactly the god-of-the-gaps argument they were expecting, and you will deserve the response you get.

audiences.startingPoint: Was taught a God who is a very powerful person in the sky, found that picture incoherent or unworthy, and left. Often carries real hurt and expects to be argued at.
audiences.approach: Agree with the rejection before offering anything. The God they left — a being inside the universe, subject to the same questions as everything in it — is one classical theism also denies, and saying so plainly is both true and disarming. Then be explicit that you are not asking them to come back to anything; you are asking whether the arguments about pure actuality are sound, which is a different question from what any institution taught them.
audiences.openingQuestion: When you stopped believing, what exactly was it that you stopped believing in? I ask because the thing Feser is defending may not be the same thing.
audiences.avoid: Do not treat the conversation as a recovery operation, and do not imply their leaving was a failure of reasoning. If they sense you are managing them rather than thinking with them, the conversation is over and you will not be told.

audiences.startingPoint: Not hostile, just unconvinced that any of this matters. Suspects philosophy is a word game that never resolves, and has limited patience for anything without a payoff.
audiences.approach: Do not start with God at all. Start with the skill: most arguments people find persuasive have a premise nobody stated, and learning to find it is useful in every part of life. Reconstruct something from the news — a policy claim, an ad — and show the hidden premise. Only then note that the same technique applied to the biggest question anyone has asked is what this book is. The payoff you are selling is clarity, not conversion.
audiences.openingQuestion: Want to see a trick? Give me any confident opinion you heard this week and I’ll find the assumption underneath it in about a minute.
audiences.avoid: Do not oversell the stakes or use the phrase ‘the most important question you’ll ever face’. Pressure reads as sales, and this listener is unusually good at detecting sales.

audiences.who: The believer who has never seen an argument
audiences.startingPoint: Believes on the basis of upbringing, community and experience; has no idea that arguments of this kind exist; may be slightly anxious that examining the question is disloyal.
audiences.approach: Distinguish natural theology from faith at the outset and treat the distinction as good news rather than a threat: the tradition has held for two thousand years that reason can reach this far on its own. Then go slowly through act and potency, because this reader often has to unlearn a personalist picture of God that the arguments will not support. Expect the classical attributes — timelessness, simplicity, immutability — to feel cold at first, and say so before they do.
audiences.openingQuestion: If someone asked you tonight why you believe God exists, and ‘because I was raised that way’ were off the table, what would you say?
audiences.avoid: Do not disparage the personalist picture as childish. It is how nearly everyone starts, including most of the tradition’s greatest figures, and mocking it makes the classical account feel like a loss rather than a discovery.

audiences.who: The analytically trained philosopher or philosophy student
audiences.startingPoint: Knows validity, soundness, modality and possible worlds; probably learned that cosmological arguments were dispatched by Hume and Kant; may regard Aristotelian metaphysics as a museum piece.
audiences.approach: Skip the hand-holding entirely and go straight to the disputed premises. Be precise about what Feser is and is not claiming: not ‘everything has a cause’, not an inference to the best explanation, not a design argument. The most productive opening is usually the difference between per se and per accidens series, followed by the question of whether the standard textbook ‘basic cosmological argument’ is a straw man — Feser argues in chapter 7 that it is, with a long pedigree running through Hume and Russell.
audiences.openingQuestion: Which premise of the argument from change do you actually reject — the principle of causality, or the impossibility of an infinite essentially ordered series?
audiences.avoid: Do not use the beginner analogies. Cup-and-desk with this audience reads as condescension, and you will lose the exchange on tone before you reach the substance.

audiences.startingPoint: Has read Dawkins or Hitchens, is confident the arguments for God are feeble, and has a set of one-line replies ready: who made God, one god further, god of the gaps, Ockham’s razor.
audiences.approach: Take the one-liners seriously and answer them one at a time, because each has a precise answer and answering them is the fastest route to credibility. ‘Who made God’ attacks a premise nobody holds. ‘One god further’ conflates a being inside the universe with the source of existence. ‘God of the gaps’ misses that the argument concerns features anything whatever must have. Then make the honest offer: you are not asking them to agree, only to attack the argument that is actually on the page.
audiences.openingQuestion: Before we start — can you state the version of the cosmological argument you think fails? I want to make sure we’re talking about the same argument.
audiences.avoid: Do not match their register. Feser himself calls some of these objections staggeringly feeble, and he has earned that after three hundred pages; borrowing the tone without the argument just produces a shouting match.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: So you’re reading a book that claims to *prove* God exists. Isn’t that a bit much? Nobody proves anything about God.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That is the claim, and I was surprised by how strong it is. Not ‘God probably exists’ or ‘God is the best explanation’ — he says these are demonstrations, like proofs in geometry. Valid arguments from premises he says are certain.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then it’s easy. Everything has a cause, God is the exception, therefore God. That argument is two thousand years old and it was dead on arrival. Who made God?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Genuinely, that’s not the argument. No premise in the book says everything has a cause. The principle is narrower: no potential gets actualized unless something already actual actualizes it.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: That sounds like the same thing in fancier words.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It isn’t, and here is the difference. ‘Everything has a cause’ applies to everything, so God would be a plain exception and you’d be right to object. The actual principle applies to potentials being actualized. Something with no potentials isn’t exempted from the rule — the rule has nothing to say about it.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Convenient. You define your conclusion so the rule can’t reach it.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It would be, if it were a definition. It’s a conclusion, and it takes fifty steps to get there. And the arguments say *why* other things need causes: they’re mixtures of what they are and what they could be. Whatever has no unrealized potentials couldn’t have a cause even in principle — there’s nothing there to be actualized.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine. But why does the chain need to stop? Why not causes all the way back? The universe might be infinitely old — plenty of cosmologists think so.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Feser grants that. Explicitly, for the sake of argument — eternal universe, multiverse, no beginning. It doesn’t affect the argument, because he isn’t arguing about that kind of chain.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: There’s another kind?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Look at your coffee. It’s off the ground because the table holds it. The table stays up because the floor does. The floor because the foundation, the foundation because the earth. Now notice: none of them has any power of its own. Take away the floor, and the table and the cup go down together — instantly, not eventually.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Sure. So?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: So compare it to your ancestors. Your grandfather caused your father, who caused you — and your grandfather can be dead. That chain doesn’t need him around any more. But the table needs the floor *right now*. Everything in the stack is borrowing.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I see the difference. But I still don’t see why the stack can’t be infinite.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Try it. A paintbrush can’t move itself. Make the handle ten feet long — still can’t. A mile. Infinitely long. Has it started painting?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Right. Length isn’t power. Everything in that stack is a borrower, and adding borrowers never produces a lender. That’s the actual claim: not that infinite series are impossible, but that a series in which nothing has power of its own explains nothing, however long.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: All right, that’s better than I expected. But suppose I grant it. You get to something at the bottom. Why call that God? Why not a quantum field, or just the way things are?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That’s the best objection you’ve made, and the book spends a whole stage of every chapter on it. The short version: a quantum field is one physical thing among others — it has states, it could have been otherwise, it has parts. So it’s a candidate for a member of the stack, not for the thing the stack rests on.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: And you get from ‘not a quantum field’ to ‘a god who cares what I do on weekends’ how, exactly?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Step by step, and each step is attackable. If it were material it would have unrealized potentials — so immaterial. If it were in time it would change — so timeless. There can’t be two, because you’d need something to tell them apart and each would then be ‘pure actuality plus something extra’. All causal power derives from it, which is what omnipotence means.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: That’s a lot of weight on ‘no unrealized potentials’.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It is. That’s exactly where I’d push if I wanted to break the argument, and I’d say so to Feser’s face. What I’d stop doing is asking who made God — that one really is aimed at a position nobody in the book holds.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Here’s my honest worry. This all feels like a machine for reaching a conclusion you already wanted.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It might be. But notice that worry is about me, not about step 12. And it cuts both ways — you don’t want the conclusion either. The only way out for either of us is to look at the premises. Which one do you actually reject?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Probably that a thing’s existing right now needs something actualizing it. Why can’t things just keep existing?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Now we’re in the right room — that’s called existential inertia, and it's one of the live debates. Chapter 1 argues against it and chapter 4 comes at it from another direction. I don’t think I can settle it for you at this table, and I’d rather admit that than bluff.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: That’s the most honest thing anyone has said to me about this.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It’s also the fastest way to find out whether the argument works. Read chapter 1 and tell me where it breaks. If you find it, I want to know.

socratic: Put your coffee on the table. What is holding it up? And what is holding that up? Keep going — where does it stop, and what would have to be true of the last thing?
If I remove the floor, when does the table fall? Now compare: if your grandfather had died before you were born, would you cease to exist? What’s different about those two cases?
A paintbrush can’t move itself. If the handle were infinitely long, could it? What exactly does length add — and what does it fail to add?
When you ask what caused your coffee, do you mean what made it twenty minutes ago, or what keeps it in existence right now? Are those the same question? Could they have different answers?

Here is hot coffee. Can it become cold? Can it become chicken soup? Can it become a live chicken? If one of those is different from the others, what does that tell you about whether ‘potential’ is just another word for nothing?
Suppose I say the book stays up because of the shelf, and the shelf stays up for no reason whatsoever — it just does, brute fact. Have I explained why the book is up there?
You know exactly what a unicorn is. Does that tell you whether any exist? What about a lion — did knowing what a lion is tell you that there are lions?
Before there were any human beings, was seven a prime number? If so, where was that truth, and what was it a truth about?
Is ‘good’ doing the same job in ‘good wine’ and ‘good man’? Is it doing a completely unrelated job, the way ‘bat’ does in two sentences? If neither — what is the third option?
You don’t believe in Zeus. What kind of thing would Zeus have been — something inside the universe, or the reason there is a universe? Does rejecting the first commit you to rejecting the second?
Suppose an argument is valid and you dislike the conclusion. What are your options? Now name every option that doesn’t involve finding a false premise.
If two intelligent people disagree about something for two thousand years, does that show neither has a proof? Would you say the same about the interpretation of quantum mechanics?
Can you picture the number seventeen? Can you reason about it correctly? What does that suggest about whether ‘I can’t picture it’ is a good objection to anything?
You’d agree a cause can’t give what it doesn’t have. Does that mean a boy needs a black eye to give one? What has to be true instead?

traps.trap: Using the word ‘cause’ without specifying which kind, so your listener silently imports the past-tense picture and hears the whole thing as an argument about the Big Bang.
traps.fix: Say ‘holding it in being right now’ before you ever say ‘cause’. Build the stack picture first; introduce the vocabulary only after they can see it.

traps.trap: Saying ‘first cause’ and leaving it undefined, so the listener pictures a starting gun.
traps.fix: Never say ‘first’ without immediately adding ‘meaning it has the power built in, not that it came earliest’. Every single time, until it becomes reflex.

traps.trap: Letting the conversation become about the age of the universe.
traps.fix: Concede it loudly and early: grant an eternal universe, a multiverse, no beginning at all. Then show that the question is untouched. Conceding is more persuasive than contesting, and it is what Feser himself does.

traps.trap: Reaching for a scientific mystery — consciousness, fine-tuning, the origin of life — as supporting evidence.
traps.fix: Don’t. You have just built a god-of-the-gaps argument on your own initiative. The whole point is that these arguments concern features anything whatever must have, not phenomena awaiting explanation.

traps.trap: Defending a God your listener already rejects — a very powerful person somewhere, with a location and a history.
traps.fix: Find out what they mean by the word in the first two minutes, and say plainly which picture you are and are not defending. Often you will find you agree with their rejection.

traps.trap: Presenting the fifty-step argument, or any long chain of steps, in conversation.
traps.fix: Nobody has ever been persuaded by a numbered list spoken aloud. Give one picture — the paintbrush — and one question, and let them do the work. Save the steps for when they ask.

traps.trap: Bluffing past a question you can’t answer because you’re afraid of losing the exchange.
traps.fix: Say ‘I don’t know, that’s in chapter 5 and I haven’t worked it through’. It costs you nothing and buys enormous credibility — and the honest version of the conversation is the only one that can actually change anyone’s mind.

traps.trap: Treating every objection as an attack to be repelled, so the exchange becomes a contest.
traps.fix: Grade objections out loud: ‘that one’s a straw man, but the one you asked before it is serious and here’s where the book takes it up’. Conceding the good ones makes your resistance to the bad ones mean something.

traps.trap: Using the beginner analogies with someone who has philosophical training.
traps.fix: Read the room. With a trained listener, name the premises and ask which they reject; cup-and-desk will read as condescension and you will lose on tone before you reach the substance.

connections.note: Read the Introduction (pages 9–15) immediately after this module. It defines natural theology, explains why the book is not about Aquinas’ Five Ways, sets out the four-part structure of every proof chapter, and previews all seven chapters. Lessons 1 and 15 here are its preparation.

The Aristotelian proof is where lessons 7 and 8 pay off. Act and potency, the principle of causality, and the distinction between linear and hierarchical series are all introduced there and used everywhere afterward. The simplified ten-step argument in this module is a compression of that chapter’s fifty steps.
The Neo-Platonic proof runs on lesson 12: composition, metaphysical parts, and what ‘simple’ means. It is also where Feser first introduces the analogical use of terms, which lesson 14 prepares.

The Augustinian proof is the direct application of lesson 11 — universals, propositions, numbers, possible worlds, and the realism/nominalism/conceptualism trio. Lesson 5 on possible worlds and lesson 6 on Plato and Augustine also feed it. Note that it is the only one of the five that is not a causal argument.

The Thomistic proof is lesson 9 in full: essence, existence, and the real distinction, plus the contingency material from lesson 5. Its conclusion — subsistent existence itself — is defined in this module’s key terms.

The rationalist proof begins from the principle of sufficient reason, which lesson 10 explains alongside the principle of causality and the case against brute facts. Lesson 4’s treatment of the fallacy of composition and lesson 5’s necessary/contingent vocabulary are also used heavily.

The first half of chapter 6 opens with three background principles — proportionate causality, agere sequitur esse, and analogy — all defined in this module’s key terms, and then derives God’s unity and simplicity. Lessons 12, 13 and 14 are its preparation; the theistic personalism material in lesson 13 comes from this part of the book.

The second half covers immutability, eternity, necessity, omnipotence, omniscience, goodness, will, love and incomprehensibility, then divine conservation and concurrence and the nature of miracles. Lesson 13’s attribute list is the map for it.

The first half of chapter 7 answers ‘what caused God?’, the straw-man ‘basic cosmological argument’, the infinite regress objection, the fallacy of composition charge and the god-of-the-gaps charge. This module’s objections section previews each in beginner’s form; lesson 4 supplies the fallacy vocabulary.

The second half covers scientism, the ‘one god further’ line, the problem of evil, divine hiddenness, and whether a controversial argument can still be a demonstration. Lesson 3 on demonstration versus probability is the key preparation for that last question.
The capstone synthesizes all five proofs and how they converge on one God. Return to this module’s distinctions and key terms before you begin it — the capstone assumes fluency in every one of them.

quiz.q: Natural theology is best defined as…
options: what can be known about God’s existence and nature by unaided reason, apart from revelation
the study of nature as a form of worship
theology based on scripture and church authority
the scientific study of religious behaviour
quiz.explanation: Feser defines it this way in the Introduction. The contrast is with revealed theology, which begins from what God is taken to have disclosed; the other options describe nature religion and the empirical study of religion.

quiz.q: An argument is valid when…
options: all of its premises are true
if its premises were true, its conclusion would have to be true
it convinces most reasonable people
its conclusion is true
quiz.explanation: Validity is a matter of form alone. ‘All cats are reptiles; Fido is a cat; so Fido is a reptile’ is valid with two false premises. Valid plus true premises is called sound.

quiz.q: Which of these is a conclusion indicator?
options: because
since
therefore
given that
quiz.explanation: ‘Therefore’ signals that what follows is being drawn from what came before. ‘Because’, ‘since’ and ‘given that’ all introduce premises.

quiz.q: Feser claims his five arguments are…
options: inferences to the best explanation
probabilistic design arguments
articles of faith supported by reason
demonstrations, whose conclusions follow necessarily from certain premises
quiz.explanation: He claims demonstration, not probability. This matters for how the arguments must be attacked: you need a false premise or an invalid step, not a rival hypothesis.

quiz.q: In Feser’s precise formulation, the principle of causality states that…
options: no potential can be actualized unless something already actual actualizes it
everything that exists has a cause
every event has a cause preceding it in time
everything has an explanation, in itself or in another
quiz.explanation: The second is the popular caricature Feser never asserts; the fourth is PSR, a distinct principle. PC concerns the actualization of potentials, which is why something with no potentials falls outside its scope.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a per accidens (linear) causal series?
options: a cup held by a desk held by a floor
a grandfather, a father, and a son
a lamp hanging from a chain from a ceiling fixture
layers of increasingly fundamental laws of nature
quiz.explanation: In a linear series, members keep their causal power once they have acted — the grandfather can be dead. The other three are hierarchical: each member’s power is derived at the moment it acts.

quiz.q: When Feser says a hierarchical series must have a ‘first’ member, ‘first’ means…
options: earliest in time
most powerful
having non-derivative causal power
occurring at the Big Bang
quiz.explanation: This is the most important terminological point in the book. A first cause has power built in rather than borrowed, which is why an infinitely long paintbrush handle still needs a painter.

quiz.q: Aristotle’s answer to Parmenides is that change does not involve something coming from nothing, because…
options: nothing really changes, only our perceptions do
change is an illusion produced by language
coming from nothing is actually possible
what comes to be was already present potentially, and a potential is not nothing
quiz.explanation: The coffee has a potential to grow cold and no potential to become chicken soup. That it has some potentials and lacks others shows potentiality is a real feature of it.

quiz.q: A substance, in Aristotle’s sense, is…
options: a thing that exists in its own right, such as this dog or this tree
a kind of material, such as bronze or water
any feature that can be predicated of something
the matter out of which a thing is made
quiz.explanation: Substance is contrasted with accident, which exists only in something else. The chemical sense of ‘substance’ as a kind of stuff is a different use of the word.

quiz.q: ‘The statue is made of bronze.’ Which of the four causes is being given?
options: formal cause
material cause
efficient cause
final cause
quiz.explanation: The material cause is what a thing is made of. The formal cause would be its statue-structure, the efficient cause the sculptor, the final cause what it is for.

quiz.q: Which distinction does the objection ‘but the universe might be infinitely old’ ignore?
options: validity versus soundness
essence versus existence
per se versus per accidens causal series
univocal versus analogical predication
quiz.explanation: Feser explicitly grants a beginningless universe for the sake of argument. The arguments concern hierarchical series operating here and now, so the age of the universe is beside the point.

quiz.q: The three arguments chapter 4 gives for the real distinction between essence and existence appeal to…
options: scripture, tradition, and reason
observation, experiment, and calculation
Plato, Aristotle, and Plotinus
knowledge, contingency, and uniqueness
quiz.explanation: You can know an essence without knowing whether it is instantiated; contingent things would be necessary if existence were part of their essence; and there could be at most one thing whose essence is existence, while ordinary kinds come in multiples.

quiz.q: PSR differs from PC in that…
options: PSR entails everything has a sufficient reason, while PC does not entail everything has a cause
PSR concerns only physical objects
PC is about explanation and PSR about causation
PC was formulated by Leibniz and PSR by Aristotle
quiz.explanation: Chapter 5 draws this contrast carefully. A cause must be distinct from its effect, but a sufficient reason need not be, so something could in principle be self-explanatory.

quiz.q: Nominalism holds that…
options: universals exist as ideas in a divine intellect
only particular things exist; universals are merely names we apply
universals exist in a realm of their own
universals exist as concepts in human minds
quiz.explanation: From Latin nomen, ‘name’. The other options describe Scholastic realism, Platonic realism and conceptualism respectively.

quiz.q: In philosophy, to call something ‘simple’ is to say that it…
options: behaves predictably
is easy to grasp
has no parts of any kind
has only one function
quiz.explanation: Philosophical simplicity is non-compositeness — no physical or metaphysical parts. Feser holds God to be incomprehensible, so simplicity is very far from ease of understanding.

quiz.q: What distinguishes theistic personalism from classical theism?
options: theistic personalism denies that God is good
classical theism denies that God exists in any sense
classical theism denies that God has intellect or will
theistic personalism takes God to fall under a genus and so to be composite rather than simple
quiz.explanation: Feser is explicit that the difference is not about whether God is personal — most classical theists attribute intellect and will to God. It is about whether God falls under a genus.

quiz.q: ‘Good wine’ and ‘a good man’ illustrate which kind of predication?
options: analogical
univocal
equivocal
metaphorical
quiz.explanation: The senses are related but not identical — the middle option between univocal (same sense) and equivocal (unrelated senses). Feser insists analogical predication is literal, not metaphorical.

quiz.q: The fallacy of composition is committed when one…
options: attacks the person rather than the argument
infers that what is true of the parts must be true of the whole
assumes the conclusion in the premises
exempts a favoured case from a general rule
quiz.explanation: ‘Every brick is light, so the wall is light.’ The other options describe ad hominem, begging the question and special pleading. Note that not all part-to-whole reasoning is fallacious — every brick being red does make the wall red.

quiz.q: Which best describes the structure of each of Feser’s first five chapters?
options: history, then argument, then application
objections, then argument, then conclusion
informal Stage 1, informal Stage 2, formal statement, objections
formal statement, informal explanation, summary
quiz.explanation: Feser describes this pattern in the Introduction. Stage 1 argues that something fitting a key description exists; Stage 2 argues that it must have the divine attributes.

quiz.q: A friend says: ‘Even if there’s a first cause, why call it God?’ Where in the book is that question answered?
options: in the objections section at the end of each chapter
in the formal numbered statement
in the Introduction
in Stage 2 of the informal statement in each proof chapter
quiz.explanation: Stage 2 exists precisely to argue that whatever fits the Stage 1 description must have unity, immateriality, eternity, omnipotence, omniscience and perfect goodness. Skipping Stage 2 leaves you unable to answer the commonest objection.

quiz.q: The infinitely long paintbrush illustrates that…
options: adding members to a hierarchical series never supplies power none of them has
infinite series are logically impossible
causes must be simultaneous with their effects
the universe must have had a beginning
quiz.explanation: Length is not power. The point is specific to hierarchical series; Feser grants that linear series might in principle be infinite.

quiz.q: Which statement about a potential is accurate?
options: a potential is simply nothing at all
a potential is a real capacity limited by what the thing actually is
everything is potentially everything else
a potential can actualize itself given enough time
quiz.explanation: Coffee is potentially cold and not potentially chicken soup. That potentials discriminate is what shows they are real features of things, and a merely potential thing cannot act — only what is actual can.

quiz.q: The principle of proportionate causality says that what is in an effect must be in its total cause…
options: only formally
only by physical transfer
formally, virtually, or eminently
only if the cause is material
quiz.explanation: The $20 example: in my wallet (formally), in my bank account (virtually), or through access to a printing press (eminently). Feser and Aquinas both reject the ‘heirloom’ reading on which the same feature must be literally handed over.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a possible world in the philosophers’ sense?
options: a world with unicorns
a world with different laws of physics
a world in which Mars has three moons
a world in which some squares are round
quiz.explanation: Possible worlds are limited by logic, not by physics. A round square is self-contradictory, so there is no such world; the other three involve no contradiction.

quiz.q: Someone objects: ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’ The most accurate response is:
options: none of the arguments uses the premise ‘everything has a cause’, and each explains why its terminus could not in principle have one
God is an exception to the rule because he is God
the rule applies only to physical things
we cannot know the answer, which is why it is called faith
quiz.explanation: Feser opens chapter 7 with this objection. It attacks a straw man, and the arguments do more than exempt their terminus — they explain why what is purely actual, or simple, or whose essence is existence, could not have had a cause.

quiz.q: Scholastic realism differs from Platonic realism in holding that universals…
options: do not exist at all
exist as ideas in a divine intellect rather than in a separate third realm
exist only in human minds
are identical with the particular things that exhibit them
quiz.explanation: Chapter 3 keeps the reality of universals and rejects Plato’s free-floating realm, on the grounds that causally inert objects standing apart from everything would be disconnected and epistemically inaccessible.

quiz.q: Feser’s central case for PSR is that…
options: it has never been observed to fail
it is true by definition
denying it is self-undermining, since one could then have no reason to think one’s beliefs track truth
it follows directly from the principle of causality
quiz.explanation: Developing Pruss and Koons, chapter 5 argues by reductio: if PSR is false, we could have no grounds for thinking we hold any belief for good reasons — including any belief that PSR is false.

quiz.q: Which of these would a metaphysical part be?
options: a chair’s legs
the atoms of a molecule
a body’s organs
the distinction between a thing’s form and its matter
quiz.explanation: Metaphysical parts are really distinct principles within one thing, not separable components. Form and matter, essence and existence, act and potency, substance and accidents are the standard cases.

quiz.q: In classical theism, God’s omnipotence is best characterized as…
options: being that from which all causal power derives
the ability to do anything describable, including contradictions
having more power than any other being
the power to intervene in nature at will
quiz.explanation: Chapter 1 derives it in steps 33–37: all power is the ability to actualize potentials, every actualization traces to the purely actual actualizer, and to be that from which all power derives is what omnipotence means.

quiz.q: You read: ‘Since every event has a physical cause, and thought is an event, thought has a physical cause.’ The premises are…
options: the second and third statements
the first two statements, with the third as conclusion
all three statements
none — this is an explanation, not an argument
quiz.explanation: ‘Since’ flags the premises; the final clause is the conclusion. Identifying which statements are doing supporting work is the first move in reading any argument.

quiz.q: The shelf-with-no-explanation example in chapter 5 is directed against…
options: the ontological argument
the reality of universals
brute facts as terminators of explanation
the principle of proportionate causality
quiz.explanation: If the shelf stays aloft as a sheer brute fact, it has no tendency of its own to stay up and so cannot impart one to the book. The same applies to a bottom-level law of nature taken as brute.

quiz.q: Which of the five proofs is NOT a causal argument?
options: the Aristotelian proof
the Thomistic proof
the rationalist proof
the Augustinian proof
quiz.explanation: Feser notes in a footnote to chapter 7 that the ‘what caused God?’ objection is not even prima facie relevant to the Augustinian proof, because unlike the others it is not a causal argument.

quiz.q: A critic argues: ‘Power and knowledge are distinct in us, so they must be distinct in God, and divine simplicity fails.’ The unstated assumption is that…
options: the terms apply univocally to God and to creatures
God exists
knowledge is a species of power
God is composite
quiz.explanation: The inference goes through only if the words mean exactly the same in both cases. Classical theists apply them analogically, which is Feser’s reply to Plantinga in chapter 6.

quiz.q: The claim that a thing continues in existence on its own once it exists, needing no sustaining cause, is called…
options: occasionalism
existential inertia
divine concurrence
the principle of plenitude
quiz.explanation: It is the main rival to divine conservation, and the name is coined by analogy with Newtonian inertia — though that analogy concerns motion rather than existence.

quiz.q: Which pair correctly matches a thinker to the proof named for him?
options: Plotinus — the argument from universals to a divine intellect
Leibniz — the argument from change to an Unmoved Mover
Aquinas — the argument from essence and existence to subsistent existence itself
Augustine — the argument from composition to an absolutely simple cause
quiz.explanation: Aquinas presented this argument in On Being and Essence. Plotinus belongs with composition and the One, Augustine with universals and the divine intellect, Leibniz with PSR and the necessary being.

quiz.q: A skeptic says: ‘Science will eventually explain everything you’re appealing to.’ The most accurate reply is:
options: science has already reached its limits
no scientific result could bear on these arguments, since science is unreliable
these arguments concern features anything whatever must have, not phenomena awaiting a mechanism
the gaps in current science are permanent
quiz.explanation: This is what distinguishes the arguments from god-of-the-gaps reasoning. A complete physics would describe how things within the world behave and would not address why anything exists or what sustains it.

quiz.q: The ‘one god further’ objection fails, on Feser’s account, because…
options: atheists have not examined every religion
Zeus might exist after all
polytheism is more coherent than monotheism
it treats the God of classical theism as a being within the universe, like Zeus, rather than the source of existence itself
quiz.explanation: Chapter 7 argues the objection rests on a category confusion. Rejecting a powerful being inside the world is a different kind of act from rejecting that in virtue of which anything exists.

quiz.q: What is a hidden premise?
options: an assumption an argument needs but does not state
a premise deliberately concealed to deceive
a conclusion drawn earlier in the text
a premise that is false
quiz.explanation: ‘He’s a politician, so he’s lying’ hides the premise that all politicians lie. Digging out the unstated assumption is usually where an argument’s real weakness turns up.

quiz.q: According to the principle agere sequitur esse…
options: every effect must resemble its cause
a thing’s activities follow from and cannot exceed its nature
action requires an external mover
being follows from action
quiz.explanation: Latin for ‘action follows being’. A stone cannot take in nutrients because that would exceed the nature of a stone; it is the formal-causal counterpart of the principle of proportionate causality.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order for working through a module of this course?
options: read the chapter, then prepare, then watch the video
watch the video, then read the chapter, then skip the practice
prepare with the module, watch the video, read the chapter, return to practise
read the chapter twice, then take the quiz
quiz.explanation: Preparation removes the vocabulary obstacle, the video orients you, the chapter supplies the argument, and returning for practice is what turns reading into understanding.

quiz.q: ‘Every part of this machine is lightweight, so the machine is lightweight.’ This is…
options: a fallacy of composition
begging the question
a straw man
an ad hominem
quiz.explanation: It moves from a property of the parts to the whole where that inference does not hold. Weight aggregates; colour does not, which is why ‘every brick is red, so the wall is red’ is fine.

quiz.q: Which best captures why a composite thing cannot account for the union of its own parts?
options: because parts always predate wholes
because to do the uniting it would have to exist already, and its existing presupposes the union
because composites have no causal powers
because the parts might be infinitely divisible
quiz.explanation: That would be an explanatory circle. Something distinct from the composite must account for its parts being united, which is the engine of chapter 2’s argument.

quiz.q: In classical theism, God’s eternity means…
options: endless duration through time
a very long lifespan
existence outside time altogether
existence from the Big Bang onward
quiz.explanation: Step 22 of chapter 1 reasons that existing in time would involve change, which pure actuality excludes. Eternity here is timelessness, not sempiternity.

quiz.q: The two — and only two — honest ways to attack a deductive argument are to…
options: question the author’s motives or point to expert disagreement
show the conclusion is unpopular or that it has bad consequences
demand more evidence or propose a rival hypothesis
show that a premise is false or that an inference does not follow
quiz.explanation: Everything else leaves the argument untouched. Proposing a rival hypothesis is appropriate against an inference to the best explanation, which is precisely what Feser claims his proofs are not.

quiz.q: ‘Mind-independent’, in the debate about universals, means independent of…
options: human minds
all minds whatsoever
physical reality
language
quiz.explanation: This is why Scholastic realism is not self-contradictory: universals can be independent of our minds while existing as ideas in a divine intellect.

quiz.q: Which question is Feser asking when he asks what causes the coffee to exist?
options: who poured it and when
what is actualizing its potential for existence at this very moment
what will eventually destroy it
what its chemical composition is
quiz.explanation: He explicitly sets aside how it got here and how it might go out of existence. The question is what keeps it in existence at any instant at which it exists.

quiz.q: Special pleading would be committed if one…
options: gave a principled reason why a case falls outside a rule
applied a rule consistently to all cases
exempted a favoured case from a general rule without a principled reason
refused to state one’s rule at all
quiz.explanation: Feser’s defence against this charge is that the arguments give the principled reason: things need causes because of a specific feature — potentiality, composition, contingency — that the terminus lacks.

quiz.q: A reader complains that she cannot picture a timeless, partless being and concludes the idea is nonsense. The best reply is:
options: imagination is the test of meaning, so the complaint stands
the idea is indeed meaningless but useful
she should try harder to visualize it
imaginability is not the test of intelligibility — one cannot picture the number seventeen either, yet reasons about it perfectly well
quiz.explanation: The intellect grasps what the imagination cannot supply a picture for; that is what distinguishes them. Chapter 6’s doctrine of divine incomprehensibility concedes that God is not exhaustively graspable while insisting that true things can be known of him.

shortAnswer.q: Explain the difference between a valid argument and a sound one, and give an example of an argument that is valid but not sound.
shortAnswer.model:
Validity concerns form alone: an argument is valid when, if its premises were true, its conclusion would have to be true. Soundness adds a further requirement — that the premises actually are true. So every sound argument is valid, but not every valid argument is sound.

An example: ‘All cats are reptiles; Fido is a cat; therefore Fido is a reptile.’ The reasoning is impeccable — given those premises, the conclusion follows necessarily — but both premises are false, so the argument establishes nothing.

The practical payoff is that it fixes the only two honest ways to attack a deductive argument: show that an inference does not follow, or show that a premise is false. Disliking the conclusion, doubting the author, or noting that clever people disagree leaves the argument untouched.
rubric: States that validity is about form: if the premises were true the conclusion would have to be true
States that soundness = validity plus actually true premises
Gives a correct example of a valid argument with a false premise
Notes that every sound argument is valid but not conversely
Draws the consequence for how deductive arguments must be attacked

shortAnswer.q: Explain the difference between a linear (per accidens) and a hierarchical (per se) causal series, with one example of each, and say why only one of them must have a first member.
shortAnswer.model:
A linear series runs backward through time and its members keep their causal power once they have acted. Your grandfather caused your father, who caused you; your grandfather can be long dead and the chain still stands. Feser grants for the sake of argument that such a series might be infinite.

A hierarchical series is different: every member except the first has its causal power only derivatively, receiving it at the moment it acts. The cup is three feet up because the desk holds it, the desk only because the floor holds the desk, the floor only because the foundation. Remove the floor and everything above it falls at once. The intermediates are like instruments — a brush does not paint, the painter paints with it.

Only the hierarchical kind must have a first member, because all its members are borrowers, and adding borrowers never produces a lender. A paintbrush cannot move itself and would not move itself if its handle were infinitely long. Note that ‘first’ here means non-derivative — having the power built in — not earliest in time.

One nuance: simultaneity is a teaching aid, not the definition. What makes a series hierarchical is the derivative character of the later members, not their sharing a moment on the clock.
rubric: Defines linear series and notes members retain their own power
Defines hierarchical series in terms of derivative or instrumental power
Gives a correct example of each
Explains why only the hierarchical kind needs a first member, using length-is-not-power reasoning
States explicitly that ‘first’ means non-derivative, not earliest
Bonus: notes that simultaneity is illustrative rather than definitional

shortAnswer.q: State the principle of causality in Feser’s precise form and explain why the difference from ‘everything has a cause’ matters.
shortAnswer.model:
Feser’s formulation is: no potential can be actualized unless something already actual actualizes it. It is step 4 of chapter 1’s formal argument.

The support is conceptual rather than merely empirical. A merely potential F cannot do anything, precisely because it is merely potential; acting is the prerogative of the actual. Potential coldness chills nothing; actual coldness does.

The difference from ‘everything has a cause’ matters enormously. If the arguments used the popular premise, then their conclusion would be an arbitrary exception and the objection ‘who made God?’ would be devastating. But they do not use it. PC applies to potentials being actualized, so something with no potentials is not exempted — the principle simply has nothing to say about it.

And the arguments go further than declining to apply the rule: they explain why the terminus could not in principle have a cause. Things need causes because they are mixtures of act and potency, or have parts to be united, or have an essence distinct from their existence, or are contingent. What is purely actual has no potentials to be actualized at all.
rubric: States PC accurately in terms of potentials and something already actual
Explains the support: only what is actual can act
Contrasts it explicitly with ‘everything has a cause’
Explains why the difference defuses the ‘who made God?’ objection
Notes that the arguments explain why the terminus could not have a cause, not merely that it does not need one

shortAnswer.q: What is natural theology, and how does it differ both from revealed theology and from empirical science?
shortAnswer.model:
Natural theology is the attempt to establish what can be known about God’s existence and nature by unaided human reason, apart from divine revelation. Feser defines it this way in the Introduction, and the whole book is an exercise in it.

It differs from revealed theology in its starting points. Revealed theology reasons from what God is taken to have disclosed — scripture, tradition, prophecy. Natural theology uses no such premise. That is why you will not find an appeal to scripture or church authority anywhere in the five proofs.

It differs from empirical science in the kind of question it asks. Science investigates how things within the world behave: what mechanisms operate, under what laws, in what order. Natural theology asks why there is anything at all, and what sustains anything in being from moment to moment. No measurement can address those questions, since any measurement presupposes something there to measure.

That second difference is also why these arguments are not god-of-the-gaps reasoning. A gaps argument points to something science has not yet explained; these arguments point to features anything whatever must have.
rubric: Defines natural theology as knowledge of God by unaided reason apart from revelation
Contrasts it with revealed theology by its starting premises
Contrasts it with science by the kind of question asked
Notes that no premise in the book is drawn from scripture or authority

shortAnswer.q: Explain actuality and potentiality using two examples, and say why Feser insists that a potential is not the same as nothing.
shortAnswer.model:
Actuality is the way a thing really is at a given moment; potentiality is a real capacity it has but is not exercising. Hot coffee is actually hot and liquid; it is potentially cold, potentially spilled, potentially a stain on the carpet. Water in a freezer is actually liquid and potentially solid.

A potential is not nothing, and the reason is that potentials discriminate. The coffee has a potential to grow cold; it has no potential to become chicken soup, to fuel a gasoline engine, or to turn into a live chicken. If potentiality were sheer nothingness, there would be nothing to distinguish the potentials a thing has from those it lacks.

This is Aristotle’s answer to Parmenides, who argued that change is impossible because the new state was nothing beforehand and something afterward, and nothing comes from nothing. Change is not something from nothing; it is the actualization of an already-real capacity.

Feser also answers the charge that potentiality is an empty concept, made by Cottingham in chapter 6. His reply is that explanations in terms of potentiality may be minimally informative, but minimally informative is not uninformative — a concept that rules things out is not empty.

Gives at least two concrete examples
Argues that potentials are real because they discriminate — some are had, others not
Connects this to Parmenides’ problem and Aristotle’s solution
Addresses or anticipates the objection that potentiality explains nothing

shortAnswer.q: What is a real distinction, how does it differ from a distinction of reason, and what are the three arguments chapter 4 gives that essence and existence are really distinct?
shortAnswer.model:
A real distinction holds in mind-independent reality; a distinction of reason reflects only our way of thinking or speaking. ‘Bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’ pick out exactly the same reality, so that distinction is one of reason. A real distinction may be between two things, or between two really distinct principles within one thing — which is the case with essence and existence.

The three arguments are these. First, from knowledge: describe lions, pterodactyls and unicorns fully to someone who has never heard of them, and he still cannot say which exists. Since both essence and existence belong to a thing’s objective reality, if they were not distinct, grasping the first would deliver the second. Second, from contingency: if a lion’s existence were included in its essence, it would exist by its very nature and so could not fail to exist. Since lions are contingent, the distinction is real. Third, from uniqueness: there could be at most one thing whose essence just is existence, since differentiating two such things would make each ‘existence itself plus something’. But ordinary kinds come in multiples, so in each of them essence and existence are distinct.

The payoff is that anything in which they are really distinct needs something conjoining them at every moment it exists — which sets a hierarchical series running toward subsistent existence itself.
rubric: Defines real distinction and contrasts it with distinction of reason with an example
Gives the argument from knowledge (lions, pterodactyls, unicorns)
Gives the argument from contingency
Gives the argument from uniqueness
States the consequence: such things need a cause conjoining essence and existence at every moment

shortAnswer.q: State the principle of sufficient reason and explain Feser’s main argument for it.
shortAnswer.model:
PSR says that everything has an explanation of why it exists and why it has the attributes it has — either in something else or in itself. Two Thomistic formulations Feser quotes are that everything which is has a sufficient reason for existing, and that everything is intelligible.

He offers an inductive case: we do in fact find explanations when we look, and even when we do not, we usually have reason to think there is one we lack access to. A world where PSR failed should be full of constantly occurring inexplicable events, and the success of science and common sense would be miraculous.

But he holds PSR is more certain than any empirical hypothesis and argues for it indirectly, by reductio. Developing Pruss and Koons: if PSR is false, there might be no connection whatever between our perceptions and the world, and no basis for calling such a disconnect improbable. Worse, we could have no reason to think we hold any belief because of good reasons rather than for no reason at all, while it falsely seemed otherwise. Since that applies to any grounds for doubting PSR, rejecting PSR is self-undermining.

He also argues that explanations terminating in brute facts are illusory: a shelf with no tendency of its own to stay aloft cannot impart such a tendency to the book on it.
rubric: States PSR accurately, including the in-itself-or-in-another disjunction
Gives the inductive support
Gives the reductio: denying PSR is self-undermining
Explains why that undercuts any argument against PSR too
Mentions the case against brute facts as explanation-terminators

shortAnswer.q: Distinguish realism, nominalism and conceptualism about universals, and explain why chapter 3 rejects two of the three.
shortAnswer.model:
Realism holds that universals — the general patterns many things share, like redness or triangularity — are real and exist independently of human minds. Nominalism holds that only particular things exist and that ‘redness’ is merely a name we apply to a group of individuals. Conceptualism holds that universals exist, but only as concepts in human minds.

Chapter 3 rejects nominalism and conceptualism on the same underlying ground: both make abstract truths depend on us. But mathematical and logical truths hold whether or not any human being thinks them. Seven was prime before there were humans and would remain so if humanity vanished. Erase every instance of ‘Snow is white’ and of ‘Schnee ist weiss’ in every language, and the proposition they expressed is still true. Names and concepts are things we make; these truths are not.

Feser also rejects Plato’s version of realism, which places universals in a third realm apart from all minds and physical things. The objection is that such objects would be causally inert and disconnected, leaving it mysterious how they relate to the world and how we could know them. The alternative, Scholastic realism, keeps universals mind-independent with respect to our minds while grounding them in a divine intellect.
rubric: Defines all three positions accurately
Gives the shared objection to nominalism and conceptualism: abstract truths do not depend on us
Supports it with an example such as mathematical truth or the proposition/sentence distinction
Explains the separate objection to Platonic realism
