shortAnswer.q: What does it mean to say that something is ‘simple’ in the philosophical sense, and why does chapter 2 argue that the ultimate cause of things must be simple?
shortAnswer.model:
Simplicity in this sense means having no parts whatsoever — not that the thing is easy to understand. And ‘parts’ is meant broadly. Besides physical parts, it includes metaphysical parts: form and matter, essence and existence, substance and accidents, actuality and potentiality, genus and specific difference.

The argument runs as follows. Anything composite depends on its parts existing and being united. This is not primarily a point about assembly over time — your organs were never made separately and bolted together, and a chair that had always existed would still depend at every moment on its parts. The composite itself cannot be what unites its parts, since it exists only given that union, which would be an explanatory circle. So something distinct from it must account for the union.

That generates a hierarchical series, which must terminate in something with no parts to be united in the first place. Hence an absolutely simple cause — what Plotinus called the One.

One important consequence: if God is simple, his power, knowledge and goodness are not three components bolted together but one reality grasped under several concepts. That is coherent only because our language about God is analogical rather than univocal.
rubric: Defines simplicity as having no parts and distinguishes it from ease of understanding
Lists metaphysical as well as physical parts
Gives the dependence argument and the explanatory-circle point
Explains that the regress terminates in something with no parts at all
Notes the consequence for the divine attributes and its connection to analogy

shortAnswer.q: Contrast classical theism with theistic personalism, and explain why the difference matters for evaluating objections to theism.
shortAnswer.model:
Classical theism holds that God is pure actuality — absolutely simple, immutable, eternal, necessary, omnipotent, omniscient and perfectly good — and is not one being among others but the source of the existence of everything else. Theistic personalism, also called neo-theism, treats God as the unique member of a species falling under the genus person, alongside human beings and angels, differing from them by lacking their limitations in power, knowledge and goodness.

It is essential to get the disagreement right. It is not that classical theists deny God is personal — most attribute intellect and will to him and regard him as personal. The dispute is whether God falls under a genus, and so is composite rather than simple. Some theistic personalists go further: process theologians such as Hartshorne deny divine immutability, but to be changeable is to have potentials as well as actualities, and so to be composite.

The difference matters because most popular objections target the personalist picture. ‘Who designed the designer?’, ‘God is an extra entity that Ockham’s razor shaves off’, and ‘you’re an atheist about every god but one’ all presuppose that God is one item in the world’s inventory, subject to the same questions as the others. Against classical theism they do not land, because the conclusion of the arguments is not another instance of existence but the source of it.
rubric: Characterizes classical theism by pure actuality and simplicity
Characterizes theistic personalism by God falling under a genus
States explicitly that the difference is not about whether God is personal
Gives at least two objections that target the personalist picture
Explains why those objections miss classical theism

shortAnswer.q: Explain univocal, equivocal and analogical predication with an example of each, and say why the distinction matters for talk about God.
shortAnswer.model:
Univocal predication uses a word in exactly the same sense in both cases: ‘Fido is a dog’ and ‘Rover is a dog’. Equivocal predication uses it in wholly unrelated senses that happen to share a spelling: the bat that flew around the attic and the bat you swung at it. Analogical predication is the middle case — related but not identical senses: ‘this wine is good’ and ‘George is a good man’.

Classical theists hold that terms applied to God are used analogically. This is not a fudge but the only remaining option once the alternatives are run out. If God-talk were univocal, God’s goodness would be the same kind of thing as human goodness — an accident of a composite, limited being — and the arguments show that such a thing needs a cause. If it were equivocal, theology would be noise and the conclusions of the proofs could not even be stated.

Two points are easy to get wrong. First, analogical predication is literal. ‘God is good’ is a true, literal claim; ‘God is a rock’ is metaphor. Feser objects specifically to the characterization of Aquinas’ view as holding that God-talk is analogical rather than literal. Second, analogy is not confined to theology — we use ‘real’ analogically of a stone and of the stone’s colour without noticing.

It matters because many objections to classical theism run on an unnoticed assumption of univocity, including Plantinga’s argument that God’s power and knowledge must be distinct because ours are.
rubric: Defines all three with a correct example of each
States that God-talk is analogical on the classical view
Explains why both extremes fail
Insists that analogical is literal, not metaphorical
Shows how the distinction defuses at least one concrete objection

shortAnswer.q: Name four fallacies the book repeatedly discusses and give an everyday example of each.
shortAnswer.model:
**Fallacy of composition** — inferring that what is true of the parts must be true of the whole. ‘Every brick is light, so the wall is light.’ Note that this is not always fallacious: every brick being red does make the wall red, so whether the inference works depends on the property.

**Begging the question** — assuming in the premises what the argument is supposed to establish. ‘This book is reliable because it says so, and what it says is true because the book is reliable.’ The argument cannot move anyone not already persuaded.

**Straw man** — refuting a weakened version of a position instead of the one actually held. Attacking ‘everything has a cause, except God’ when no proponent of these arguments holds it. Feser argues in chapter 7 that the textbook ‘basic cosmological argument’ is exactly this, with a long pedigree.

**Special pleading** — exempting a favoured case from a general rule without a principled reason. ‘Everything needs a cause, except God, because he’s God.’ Feser’s defence is that the arguments supply the principled reason: things need causes because of a feature — potentiality, composition, contingency — that the terminus lacks.

A fifth worth knowing is **god of the gaps**: invoking God to fill a hole in current science, so that the explanation dies when the hole is filled.
rubric: Names at least four of composition, begging the question, straw man, special pleading, god of the gaps, ad hominem
Gives a correct everyday example of each named
Explains why each pattern fails
Connects at least two to how they arise in debates about these arguments
Bonus: notes that part-to-whole reasoning is not always fallacious

shortAnswer.q: A friend says: ‘Even if your argument works, you’ve only got some abstract first cause. Why call that God?’ How should you answer, and where does the book handle it?
shortAnswer.model:
This is the strongest of the beginner-level objections and deserves to be taken seriously rather than brushed aside. The book handles it in Stage 2 of the informal statement in each of the first five chapters — which is exactly why skipping Stage 2 leaves readers unable to answer the objection they will meet most often.

The strategy is to show that anything fitting the Stage 1 description must, by the same metaphysics, have further features. If it were material it would have unactualized potentials, so it is immaterial. If it were in time it would change, so it is eternal. There could not be two, since differentiating them would make each ‘pure actuality plus something’, so it is unique. All causal power derives from it, which is what omnipotence means. The patterns of everything it causes must be present in it somehow, and in a purely actual immaterial cause they can only be present in the manner of intellect — hence omniscience. To fall short of goodness is to fail to actualize something, and there is no such failure, hence perfect goodness.

A rival candidate such as a quantum field fails because it is one physical thing among others, with states, parts and potentials — a candidate for a member of the series, not its terminus.

Be honest about the limits, though. Natural theology does not deliver any particular revealed religion, and Feser says so in the Introduction: he thinks the real debate begins where natural theology leaves off.
rubric: Identifies Stage 2 of each proof chapter as where this is answered
Describes the general strategy: the same metaphysics yields the further attributes
Gives at least three specific derivations
Explains why a physical candidate such as a quantum field fails
Acknowledges honestly what natural theology does not deliver

shortAnswer.q: Why does Feser insist his proofs are demonstrations rather than probabilistic arguments, and what difference does that make to how they should be criticized?
shortAnswer.model:
A demonstration is a valid deductive argument from premises that are certain; its conclusion follows necessarily. An inference to the best explanation, by contrast, accepts the hypothesis that accounts for the evidence better than its rivals, and yields a conclusion that is probable and defeasible.

Feser claims demonstration, and the claim is not modest: in the Introduction he says a long line of thinkers held that God’s existence can be rationally demonstrated by purely philosophical arguments, and that the aim of his book is to show they were right.

The difference matters for criticism. Against a best-explanation argument, it is fair to say ‘some other hypothesis might do better’, ‘science may yet find a natural cause’, or ‘this is a god-of-the-gaps move’. Against a purported demonstration these replies are beside the point, because the argument does not rest on being the best available account of some phenomenon. There are only two ways in: show that a premise is false, or show that an inference does not follow.

This is also why the objection sections matter so much. They are where Feser states the best attempts to do exactly those two things, and they are the fastest route to finding out whether the arguments survive.
rubric: Defines demonstration and contrasts it with inference to the best explanation
Notes that Feser explicitly claims the stronger status
Explains that rival-hypothesis and gaps objections are appropriate only to the weaker kind
States the two legitimate lines of attack
Connects this to the role of the objection sections

shortAnswer.q: Describe the structure of each of Feser’s first five chapters and give practical advice for reading a fifty-step formal argument without panic.
shortAnswer.model:
Each of the first five chapters has four parts. First, an informal statement in Stage 1, arguing discursively that something fitting a key description exists. Second, an informal Stage 2, arguing that anything fitting that description must have the divine attributes. Third, a formal statement setting the reasoning out as explicit numbered steps. Fourth, objections — which Feser notes are in some cases the most technical material in the chapter.

For the numbered argument, four habits help. First, remember it is a recap: it introduces no material the informal pages have not already supplied, so a baffling step is explained earlier. Second, find the joints — in chapter 1, steps 1–5 establish change and the principle of causality, 6–14 run the hierarchical-series argument to a purely actual actualizer, 15–18 establish uniqueness, and 19–47 derive the attributes. Read four blocks, not fifty steps. Third, label every step as premise, inference or conclusion; steps beginning ‘So’ are inferences and need only a valid link, so the weight is on the premises. Fourth, attack rather than absorb: after each block, ask which single step you would challenge first.

It also helps to know what can wait. Feser starts at the shallow end and ends in the deep end by design, so difficulty near the end of a chapter is the structure working, not a personal failure. The science-based objections in chapter 1 can be skimmed on a first read and returned to.
rubric: Names all four parts of a proof chapter in order
Explains what Stage 1 and Stage 2 each secure
Gives at least three concrete reading tactics for the formal argument
Notes that the formal statement is a recap of the informal pages
Mentions that difficulty increases by design and what can be deferred

shortAnswer.q: Someone objects that these arguments are god-of-the-gaps reasoning. Explain why Feser denies this, and what would make an argument genuinely of that kind.
shortAnswer.model:
A god-of-the-gaps argument points to something current science has not explained and proposes God as the filler. Its weakness is structural: the explanation dies as soon as the gap closes, so the position retreats with every advance.

Feser denies that his arguments have this form, and addresses the charge in chapter 7 around page 271. The reason is that they do not rest on any gap in scientific knowledge. They begin from features that anything whatever must have: that it changes, that it has parts, that its essence is not its existence, that it is contingent. No account of mechanism could address these, because any mechanism you propose has the very same features and so raises the same question.

This is also why the arguments are indifferent to cosmology. Feser grants a beginningless universe or multiverse for the sake of argument. An argument that needed the universe to have had a beginning would indeed be hostage to future physics; his is not.

The practical lesson for anyone defending the arguments is to avoid citing scientific mysteries — consciousness, fine-tuning, the origin of life — as support. Doing so converts a demonstration into precisely the gaps argument the objector was expecting.
rubric: Defines god-of-the-gaps reasoning and states why it is weak
Explains that the arguments start from universal features rather than unexplained phenomena
Notes that any proposed mechanism has the same features
Connects this to Feser’s granting of a beginningless universe

shortAnswer.q: Explain the principle of proportionate causality using the $20 example, and say how Feser answers the charge that it is refuted by counterexamples like sponge cake.
shortAnswer.model:
PPC says that whatever is in an effect must in some way be in its total cause — a cause cannot give what it does not have. The ‘in some way’ is crucial, and the $20 example unpacks it. If I give you $20, I might have the bill in my wallet and hand it over: what is in the effect was in the cause **formally**. Or I might have no cash but $20 in the bank and wire it: it was in the total cause — me plus my account — **virtually**, as a power to obtain it. Or I might have access to a Federal Reserve printing press and have a bill run off: it was there **eminently**, as a more fundamental power to make such bills.

Cottingham objects that a sponge cake has sponginess that was in none of its ingredients, and that helium has properties hydrogen lacked. Feser gives three replies. First, the objection restricts PPC to material factors, when the principle concerns the *total* cause — which is itself a straw man. Second, the ‘heirloom’ reading, on which the same feature must literally be handed over, is one defenders of PPC explicitly reject; as one Thomist puts it, a boy need not have a black eye to give one. Third, Cottingham grants that the sponginess emerges from the chemical changes but complains that saying it was potentially present makes PPC trivial. Feser replies that explanations in terms of potentiality may be minimally informative, but minimally informative is not trivial or uninformative.

He adds that naturalist philosophers use PPC implicitly — Churchland argues that purely material beginnings plus purely material processes yield a purely material result, which assumes exactly this principle.
rubric: States PPC accurately including the ‘total cause’ qualification
Explains formally, virtually and eminently with the $20 example
States Cottingham’s counterexample fairly
Gives at least two of Feser’s replies, including the rejection of the heirloom reading
Bonus: notes that naturalist philosophers use the principle implicitly

shortAnswer.q: A friend says: ‘Philosophers have argued about this for 2,500 years without agreement, so nobody has a proof.’ Evaluate this reasoning.
shortAnswer.model:
The premise is true and the inference does not follow.

First, the argument proves too much. Informed, intelligent people still disagree about whether mathematical objects exist, whether determinism is true, and how to interpret quantum mechanics. Nobody concludes that these questions have no answers or that the arguments about them are worthless.

Second, and more fundamentally, an argument’s force is not settled by a head-count. A demonstration is refuted by a false premise or an invalid step, not by a survey of opinion. Feser takes this up at the close of chapter 7 (around page 307), arguing that a conclusion’s being controversial does not entail that the argument for it fails as a demonstration. If it did, a valid proof would cease to be one the moment someone clever refused to accept it.

Third, the picture of philosophy as making no progress is inaccurate. It progresses by ruling out positions, sharpening distinctions and exposing bad arguments rather than by producing unanimity — and much of chapter 7 is exactly that kind of work.

What the objection does get right is that persistent expert disagreement is a reason for intellectual humility about one’s own confidence. That is a fair conclusion; ‘therefore nobody has a proof’ is not.
rubric: Identifies that the inference from disagreement to failure does not follow
Gives a parallel case where we do not draw that conclusion
States that demonstrations are refuted by premises and inferences, not head-counts
Notes where Feser addresses this (end of chapter 7)
Concedes what is legitimate in the objection

flashcards.back: What can be known about God’s existence and nature by unaided human reason, apart from divine revelation. The discipline this whole book belongs to.
Theology that reasons from what God is taken to have disclosed — scripture, tradition, prophecy. No premise in the five proofs comes from here.
A premise is a reason offered in support; the conclusion is what the reasons are meant to establish. Premise indicators: because, since, given that. Conclusion indicators: therefore, so, hence, thus.
An assumption an argument needs but does not state. ‘He’s a politician, so he’s lying’ hides ‘all politicians lie.’ Digging it out is usually where the real weakness turns up.
If the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true. A matter of form only — ‘All cats are reptiles; Fido is a cat; so Fido is a reptile’ is valid.
Valid plus all premises actually true. Every sound argument is valid; not every valid argument is sound.

flashcards.front: The only two honest ways to attack a deductive argument
flashcards.back: Show that a premise is false, or show that an inference does not follow. Nothing else touches it.
Reasoning in which the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises. If the premises are true, the conclusion cannot be false.
Reasoning from observed cases to a general conclusion. True premises make the conclusion probable, not guaranteed.
Accepting a hypothesis because it explains the evidence better than rivals. Probable and defeasible — and not what Feser claims to be doing.
A valid deductive argument from premises that are certain. This is the strong claim Feser makes for all five proofs.

flashcards.front: Why the demonstration claim changes how you criticize
flashcards.back: ‘Some other explanation might work’ and ‘science may yet find a cause’ are fair against best-explanation arguments and beside the point against a demonstration.
Inferring that what is true of the parts is true of the whole. ‘Every brick is light, so the wall is light.’ Not always fallacious — every brick being red does make the wall red.
Assuming in the premises the very thing to be proved. ‘The book is reliable because it says so, and what it says is true because the book is reliable.’
Refuting a weakened version of a position instead of the one actually held — e.g. attacking ‘everything has a cause, except God’, which nobody in this book holds.
Exempting a favoured case from a rule without a principled reason. Feser’s defence: the arguments supply the reason — the terminus lacks the feature that makes other things need causes.
Invoking God to fill a hole in current science, so the explanation dies when the hole closes. Feser denies his arguments have this form (ch. 7, around p. 271).
Attacking the arguer rather than the argument. ‘You only believe that because of your upbringing’ says nothing about whether the premises are true.
Exists, but could have failed to exist. You, the moon, lions. Not the everyday sense of ‘conditional on’.
Something whose existence is explained by its own nature and which could not have failed to exist. The conclusion of the rationalist proof.
A complete, non-contradictory way things could have been — not a place or a parallel universe. Limited by logic, not by physics.
A substance exists in its own right (this dog). An accident exists only in something else (the dog’s brownness). Not the everyday sense of ‘accident’ as mishap.
Matter is the stuff; form is the organizing pattern making it that kind of thing. The same bronze can have the form of a statue or of a doorstop.
Material (what it’s made of), formal (what it is), efficient (what brought it about), final (what it’s for). A chair: wood, chair-structure, carpenter, being sat on.
The way a thing really is right now. Only what is actual can do anything — potential coldness chills nothing.
A real capacity a thing has but isn’t exercising, limited by what it actually is. Coffee is potentially cold, not potentially chicken soup.
Because potentials discriminate: the coffee has some and lacks others. A concept that rules things out is not empty. This is Aristotle’s answer to Parmenides.
Change would mean the new state came from nothing, which is impossible — so change is impossible. Answer: it came from a potential, which is not nothing.
The actualization of a potential. Covers qualitative (coffee cooling), local (leaf falling), quantitative (puddle growing) and substantial (fly dying) change.
Whatever actualizes a potential — including what sustains a thing in being right now, not only what got it started in the past.

flashcards.front: The two questions about a thing
flashcards.back: How did it get here? (past, historical) versus What keeps it in existence at this instant? (here-and-now). Feser almost always asks the second.
Runs back through time; members keep their power once they have it. Grandfather → father → son. Feser grants it might in principle be infinite.
Every member but the first has power only derivatively, received at the moment it acts. Cup → desk → floor → foundation → earth.
Not simultaneity — that’s just a teaching aid. It is the derivative, instrumental character of the later members.
Non-derivative — having causal power built in rather than borrowed. NOT earliest in time, NOT the Big Bang.
A brush can’t move itself, and wouldn’t if its handle were infinitely long. Length isn’t power; adding borrowers never produces a lender.

flashcards.front: Why ‘maybe the universe is infinitely old’ misses
flashcards.back: Feser explicitly grants a beginningless universe or multiverse for the sake of argument. The proof concerns hierarchical, here-and-now series.
A cause with only borrowed power, like a tool. A brush doesn’t paint — the painter paints with it. Desk, floor and foundation are instruments of the earth.
No potential can be actualized unless something already actual actualizes it. Step 4 of chapter 1. It does NOT say ‘everything has a cause’.
Everything has an explanation of why it exists and is as it is — in something else, or in itself. Equivalently: everything is intelligible.
A cause must be distinct from its effect; a reason need not be, so something could be self-explanatory. PSR entails everything has a reason; PC does not entail everything has a cause.
Reductio: if PSR is false, we could have no reason to think we hold beliefs for good reasons — which applies to any case against PSR too. The denial is self-undermining.
A fact with no explanation at all. If the shelf stays aloft as a brute fact, it has no tendency of its own to stay up, so it can’t impart one to the book. The explanation is illusory.
Whatever is in an effect must be in its TOTAL cause somehow — formally, virtually, or eminently. A cause can’t give what it hasn’t got.
The $20: in my wallet (formally), in my bank account (virtually), or via access to a printing press (eminently).
The same feature needn’t be literally handed over — a boy needn’t have a black eye to give one. It need only be in the total cause in some way.
‘Action follows being’: a thing’s activities follow from and cannot exceed its nature. A stone cannot take in nutrients.
What a thing is — its nature, the answer to ‘what kind of thing is this?’ A human being, traditionally, is a rational animal.
The fact that a thing is, as opposed to what it is. You can grasp what a unicorn is and know that there are none.

flashcards.front: Real distinction vs. distinction of reason
flashcards.back: A real distinction tracks mind-independent reality; a distinction of reason is only in our thinking — ‘bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’ pick out the same thing.

flashcards.front: Argument from knowledge for the real distinction
flashcards.back: Describe lions, pterodactyls and unicorns fully to someone unfamiliar with all three; he still can’t say which exists. So essence doesn’t deliver existence.

flashcards.front: Argument from contingency for the real distinction
flashcards.back: If a lion’s existence were part of its essence, it would exist by its very nature and couldn’t fail to exist. Lions are contingent, so the distinction is real.

flashcards.front: Argument from uniqueness for the real distinction
flashcards.back: There could be at most one thing whose essence just is existence — differentiating two would make each ‘existence itself PLUS something’. Ordinary kinds come in multiples.
That whose essence just is existence — the conclusion of the Thomistic proof. Latin: ipsum esse subsistens. It can impart existence without receiving it.
A general pattern many particular things exhibit — redness, triangularity, humanness. The pattern, not the collection of instances.
Real, but not in space or time, and not causally interacting: universals, propositions, numbers, possible worlds. Not ‘vague’ or ‘imaginary’.
‘Snow is white’ and ‘Schnee ist weiss’ are two sentences expressing one proposition. Erase both and the proposition is still true.
Realism: universals are real independently of us. Nominalism: only particulars exist; universals are just names. Conceptualism: universals are concepts in human minds.

flashcards.front: Why ch. 3 rejects nominalism and conceptualism
flashcards.back: Both make abstract truths depend on us. But seven was prime before humans existed and would be if humanity vanished. Names and concepts are things we make.
Universals are mind-independent with respect to OUR minds, but exist as ideas in a divine intellect — not in a Platonic third realm.
Made of parts — physical or metaphysical. A composite depends at every moment on its parts existing and being united.
Really distinct principles within one thing, not separable objects: form/matter, essence/existence, substance/accidents, act/potency, genus/difference.

flashcards.front: Why a composite can’t unite its own parts
flashcards.back: It exists only given that union, so explaining the union by it would be an explanatory circle. Something distinct from it must account for the union.
Having NO parts of any kind. Not ‘easy to understand’ — Feser holds God to be incomprehensible, and simplicity is a large part of why.
God as pure actuality: simple, immutable, eternal, necessary, omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good — the source of existence, not a being among beings.
God as the unique member of a species under the genus person — immensely powerful, but composite. The recent departure, not the tradition.
…whether God is personal. Most classical theists attribute intellect and will to God. The dispute is whether God falls under a genus and is composite.
No unrealized potentials whatever. The conclusion of the Aristotelian proof, and the root from which nearly every other divine attribute is derived.

flashcards.front: How the divine attributes are derived
flashcards.back: One repeating pattern: attribute X would require an unactualized potential; pure actuality has none; therefore not-X. Steps 19–32 of chapter 1.
Outside time altogether, not endless duration. Existing in time would involve change, which pure actuality excludes.
Being that from which ALL causal power derives — not ‘can do anything describable, including contradictions’.
The world could not exist even for an instant unless God were continually sustaining it in being. The opposite of deism.
The rival thesis that once a thing exists it simply continues on its own, needing no sustaining cause. Named by analogy with Newtonian inertia.
Univocal: same sense (‘Fido is a dog’ / ‘Rover is a dog’). Equivocal: unrelated (bat in the attic / bat in your hand). Analogical: related but not identical (‘good wine’ / ‘good man’).
‘God is good’ is a literal claim used analogically. ‘God is a rock’ is metaphor. Feser objects to calling Aquinas’ view ‘analogical rather than literal’.
Many attacks on divine simplicity assume univocity — e.g. ‘power and knowledge are distinct in us, so must be in God.’ Analogy blocks the inference.
No argument uses ‘everything has a cause’. And each explains why its terminus couldn’t have a cause: it has no potentials, no parts, no essence distinct from existence, no contingency.

flashcards.front: Reply to ‘why can’t the regress be infinite?’
flashcards.back: For linear series, Feser agrees it might be. For hierarchical series, every member is a borrower, and no number of borrowers produces a lender.
Zeus is a powerful being inside the universe; classical theism’s God is the source of existence itself. Rejecting the first doesn’t commit you to rejecting the second (ch. 7, pp. 289–292).
Science asks how things within the world behave; these arguments ask why anything exists and what sustains it. A finished physics wouldn’t touch the question.

flashcards.front: Reply to ‘isn’t this just faith dressed up?’
flashcards.back: That’s an ad hominem about arguers, not arguments. Natural theology uses no premise from revelation, and the arguments tell you exactly how to refute them.
Demonstrations are refuted by false premises or invalid steps, not by head-counts. Feser addresses whether a proof can be controversial at the end of ch. 7 (p. 307).
Imaginability isn’t the test of intelligibility. You can’t picture the number seventeen or a thousand-sided polygon, yet you reason about both rigorously.
1. Informal Stage 1 (something fitting a description exists). 2. Informal Stage 2 (it must have the divine attributes). 3. Formal numbered statement. 4. Objections.
Answering ‘even if there’s a first cause, why call it God?’ — the objection you’ll meet most often. Skipping Stage 2 leaves you unable to answer it.
It’s a recap, not new material. Break into blocks (1–5 setup, 6–14 to pure actuality, 15–18 uniqueness, 19–47 attributes). Label each step. Ask which one you’d challenge.
These are inferences. They need only a valid link to earlier steps — the independent defence belongs to the premises, which is where you should spend your attention.

flashcards.front: The five thinkers and their questions
flashcards.back: Aristotle: how is change possible? Plotinus: what holds parts together? Augustine: where do the patterns live? Aquinas: why does anything exist? Leibniz: why anything rather than nothing?

flashcards.front: What Feser says his book is NOT
flashcards.back: Not a book about Aquinas’ Five Ways, not textual exegesis of anyone, and not preceded by a long metaphysical prolegomenon — the background is introduced as needed.
The claim that science is the only source of knowledge. Self-defeating, since the claim itself isn’t a scientific result. Chapter 7 develops this from around p. 273.
Leibniz: each copy is explained by the previous copy, infinitely. Yet why the series contains geometry at all is untouched. Used against the fallacy-of-composition charge.

teachBack:
**The challenge.** Explain the difference between a linear and a hierarchical causal series to a real human being who has never studied philosophy — a friend, a sibling, a colleague at lunch — in under five minutes, using nothing but objects within arm’s reach.

**The constraints, and they matter.**

- No jargon at all. You may not say *per se*, *per accidens*, *actualize*, *potency*, *contingent*, or *metaphysics*. If you need a technical word, define it in ordinary language first and then use the ordinary version.
- You must use a physical object they can see. Put something on a table and work from there.
- You must get them to say out loud why the stack needs something with power of its own. If you say it for them, you have failed the exercise.
- You may not mention God. This is an exercise about causal structure, and smuggling in the conclusion will make your listener defensive and teach you nothing about whether the explanation worked.

**How to check yourself.** Afterwards, ask them two questions. First: ‘give me your own example of each kind of chain.’ If the examples are good, the idea landed; if they hand back your cup and desk, it didn’t. Second: ‘if the stack had a million things in it instead of four, would that change anything?’ If they say no and can say why, you have taught it. If they hesitate, go back to the paintbrush.

**The harder version, once you can do the first.** Same exercise, but your listener is allowed to interrupt with the three standard objections — ‘maybe it’s infinite’, ‘maybe the universe is eternal’, ‘who holds up the last thing’ — and you must answer each without notes and without raising your voice.

**A written version, if no victim is available.** Write two paragraphs. The first explains the distinction to a curious twelve-year-old. The second explains it to someone with a physics degree who suspects this is medieval nonsense. Then compare them: the second should not be longer or more technical, only differently addressed. If you needed more jargon for the physicist, you probably don’t understand it yet.

**Why this particular challenge.** Feser’s five arguments diverge in their starting points and converge in their conclusion, and of everything in this primer, this one distinction is doing the most work in the most chapters. If you can teach it cold, chapter 1 will read like a summary of things you already know — which is exactly the state you want to be in on page 17.
videoPrompt:
Audience: an adult who has never taken a philosophy class and is about to read Edward Feser’s *Five Proofs of the Existence of God* for the first time. They are curious and intelligent but have no background at all, and they are slightly intimidated. Tone: warm, patient, unhurried, concrete — a good tutor at a kitchen table, never a lecturer. Do not argue for or against God’s existence; this is orientation, not persuasion.

Cover the ideas in this order and give each one time: (1) what philosophy and natural theology are, and how natural theology differs from faith and from science; (2) how to find the premises and conclusion inside ordinary prose, and what validity and soundness mean; (3) actuality and potentiality, using the cooling coffee — stressing that coffee can become cold but not chicken soup; (4) the difference between a linear chain of causes running back through time and a hierarchical stack of causes operating right now, using the cup on the desk on the floor, and the infinitely long paintbrush. Spend the most time here: it is the single most important idea. (5) essence versus existence, using lions, pterodactyls and unicorns; (6) what classical theism means — pure actuality, simplicity, timelessness — as against a very powerful being inside the universe.

Correct these misconceptions explicitly: that the arguments assume ‘everything has a cause’; that ‘first cause’ means earliest in time; that the arguments depend on the universe having had a beginning; and that ‘simple’ means easy to understand. End by describing the four-part shape of every proof chapter — informal stage 1, informal stage 2, formal numbered steps, objections — and reassuring the listener that a fifty-step argument is always a recap of pages they will already have read.

readingGuide.beforeYouRead:
This is the very first stop in the course, and it is designed for someone who has never taken a philosophy class. You do not need to believe in God, disbelieve in God, or know anything about Aristotle to begin. You only need curiosity and a willingness to go slowly.

**What this module is for.** Feser’s book defends five arguments that God exists. Each argument uses a few specialized tools — words like *potentiality*, *essence*, *contingent*, *hierarchical series*. Feser explains them as he goes, but quickly. This module teaches those tools in advance, one at a time, with ordinary examples (coffee cooling, a cup on a desk, a $20 bill), so that when you meet them in the book they feel like old friends.

**How to use the whole course.** Every module follows the same rhythm, and it works best in this order:

1. **Preview** the module here: read the plain-English box at the top of each lesson, then the full lesson, then try the quick checks.
2. **Watch** the module’s video (made in NotebookLM from the module’s study document) for a relaxed overview.
3. **Read** the chapter in the book, using the reading map for that module to know where to slow down.
4. **Return** to the module for practice: the argument walk-through, objections, quiz, flashcards, and the teach-back challenge.

This primer is the one exception: there is no book chapter to read afterward. Instead, when you finish it you will read Feser’s short Introduction (pages 9–15) and then chapter 1.

**What you will be asked to accept.** Nothing, yet. This module explains ideas; it does not require you to agree with them. You will learn how Feser uses words, why he thinks his arguments are more than guesses, and what he means by “God.” Whether his arguments succeed is something you will judge for yourself chapter by chapter.

**Reassurance about the hard parts.** Two lessons carry most of the weight: lesson 7 (act and potency) and lesson 8 (hierarchical versus linear causal series). If they feel slippery, that is normal — philosophers took centuries to state them carefully. Read them twice, try the examples with objects on your own desk, and do not move on until you can explain the cup–desk–floor example out loud. Everything else in the book gets easier once those two ideas click.

knowFirst.plain: A set of reasons (premises) offered to support a claim (the conclusion). In philosophy an argument is not a quarrel; it is a chain of reasoning you can inspect link by link.

An argument is valid when its conclusion really follows: if the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true. Validity is about the shape of the reasoning, not whether the premises are actually true.
A deductive argument whose conclusion follows necessarily from premises that are certain. This is what Feser claims his proofs are — not ‘probably God,’ but ‘God, necessarily, given these premises.’
Something that exists but could have failed to exist, like you, a tree, or the moon. The opposite of necessary.
A real capacity a thing has but is not using yet: hot coffee can become cold; it cannot become chicken soup. Aristotle’s word for ‘what a thing can be.’
The way a thing actually is right now: the coffee’s actual heat, your actual reading of this sentence. Only something actual can make a potential become actual.

A chain of causes where every link works only because the link above it is working at the same time — a cup held up by a desk, held up by a floor, held up by the earth. This kind of chain must have a first member with power of its own.
What a thing is — its nature, what makes it the kind of thing it is (a triangle is a closed three-sided figure). Different from the fact that it exists.
The principle that everything has an explanation — either in itself or in something else. Nothing is simply there for no reason at all.
The traditional view of God defended in the book: not a big being in the universe but pure actuality — simple, unchanging, timeless, the source of the existence of everything else.

questionsToHold: When Feser says he has a “proof,” what exactly is he claiming — certainty, high probability, or something else? What would count as refuting it?
Is a potential “nothing,” or is it a real feature of things? What would follow if it were nothing at all?
When I ask what caused something, am I asking about its past (what got it started) or its present (what keeps it going right now)?
Could a chain of things that each have only borrowed power explain anything, however long the chain is?
Does the word “God” in this debate mean the same thing to believers and skeptics? What would each side need to agree on before arguing?
Can a word like “good” or “cause” mean something true of God without meaning exactly what it means of a person or a machine?

map.what: Feser explains what natural theology is, why this is not a commentary on Aquinas’ Five Ways, how every proof chapter is built (informal Stage 1, informal Stage 2, formal statement, objections), previews all seven chapters, and makes the bold claim that the proofs succeed and that the real debate is among different kinds of theists.
map.tip: Read it in one sitting right after finishing this primer. Underline the definition of natural theology and the two-stage description of each proof; you will use both constantly.

map.what: From the fact of change to a purely actual actualizer (the Unmoved Mover). Introduces act and potency, the principle of causality, linear versus hierarchical series, and derives the divine attributes. Then a 50-step formal statement and long objection sections (Hume, Kant, Russell, Newton, Einstein, quantum mechanics).
map.tip: Pages 17–29 are the heart of the whole book: go slowly and reread the cup–desk–floor pages (21–26). The science-based objections (pages 43–63) can be skimmed on a first read and revisited later.

map.what: Things made of parts need something to hold their parts together here and now; the regress ends in something absolutely simple, Plotinus’ “the One.” Introduces metaphysical parts (form and matter, essence and existence) and the analogical use of language.
map.tip: Short and elegant. Slow down where Feser explains how many divine attributes can belong to one simple reality — lesson 12 of this primer prepares you for it.

map.what: Universals, propositions, numbers, and possible worlds are real but are neither physical things nor mere human ideas; the only adequate ground for them is an eternal divine intellect. Covers realism, nominalism, conceptualism, and three kinds of realism.
map.tip: Review lesson 11 first. The six arguments for realism (pages 90–92) are worth outlining in your notes; the later objections (Leftow, Grim) can be read lightly the first time.

map.what: In every ordinary thing, what it is (essence) is really distinct from the fact that it is (existence); such things need a cause that conjoins their essence and existence at every moment, ending in something whose essence just is existence — subsistent existence itself.
map.tip: Master the three arguments for the real distinction (pages 117–122) before going on. Kenny’s objection (pages 135–141) is the most technical passage; read it last.

map.what: Defends the principle of sufficient reason and argues that contingent things can only be ultimately explained by a necessary being whose existence is explained by its own nature. Discusses brute facts, infinite series, and the fallacy of composition.
map.tip: Very readable. Pay close attention to why PSR is not the same as the principle of causality (page 148) and to the geometry-book example (pages 155–157).

map.section: Chapter 6: The Nature of God and of His Relationship to the World
map.what: The longest chapter: three background principles (proportionate causality, agere sequitur esse, analogy), then God’s unity, simplicity, immutability, eternity, necessity, omnipotence, omniscience, goodness, will, love, incomprehensibility; then conservation, concurrence, and miracles. In this course it is split into two modules (6A: pages 169–205; 6B: pages 205–248).
map.tip: Do not read it in one go. Lessons 13 and 14 of this primer (classical theism, analogy) are your preparation. Take a break after the section on eternity and necessity (around page 208).

map.section: Chapter 7: Common Objections to Natural Theology
map.what: Answers the popular objections: “What caused God?”, the straw-man “basic cosmological argument,” infinite regress, the fallacy of composition, god of the gaps, scientism, “one god further,” the problem of evil, divine hiddenness, and whether something controversial can be a proof. Split in this course into 7A (pages 249–273) and 7B (pages 273–308).
map.tip: The most conversational chapter and very useful for real discussions. The section on scientism (pages 273–286) repays careful study; the evil and hiddenness sections should be read slowly and with patience.

afterReading: Without looking, explain the difference between a potential and an actuality using an example from your own kitchen.
Draw the cup–desk–floor–earth stack and the grandfather–father–son line side by side, and explain in two sentences why only the stack needs a first member.
State the principle of causality in Feser’s exact form (not “everything has a cause”) and explain why that difference defuses “Who made God?”
Take a short opinion article and mark its conclusion, its premises, one hidden premise, and any indicator words.
Explain to an imaginary friend why a demonstration is attacked differently from a scientific hypothesis.
List four attributes of God in classical theism and explain why a “very powerful being inside the universe” would not have them.
Explain what the word “good” means in “good wine” and “good man,” and why that is analogy rather than equivocation.
If you can do all of the above, you are ready for the Introduction (pages 9–15) and chapter 1.
